analysis_zh.research_question_and_background: 本研究旨在评估在新生儿泌尿道感染(UTI)患者中使用短期静脉抗生素疗程(≤4天)的可行性及安全性。背景资料显示,UTI是60天以下婴儿住院的主要原因之一,约有10–20%的发热发作与之相关。
analysis_zh.study_design_and_population: 一项回顾性单中心队列研究研究在大学特鲁索医院进行,纳入了住院治疗的<28天新生儿,其尿路感染(UTI)经培养确诊。该队列研究共包含138例患者,其中82%为男性,中位年龄为15.5天,根据临床严重程度、菌血症、肾盂输尿管扩张或ESBL感染分为低风险组或高风险组。
analysis_zh.methods: 收集了人口统计学、临床、实验室、影像学以及治疗数据。临床严重程度根据外周灌注不足的迹象、是否需要补液复苏或是否入住重症监护病房进行评估。统计分析包括定量变量的描述性统计和正态分布的Shapiro-Wilk检验。
analysis_zh.main_results: 共有138例患者被纳入研究;82%为男性,中位年龄为15.5天。其中,97例(71%)被归类为低风险,95例(98%)接受了短期静脉抗生素治疗。70%的患者出现发热,其中17%在入院前发热超过12小时。43%的患者血清降钙素原升高(>0.5 μg/L),包括37%无严重感染风险因素的患者。
analysis_zh.interpretation_and_novelty: 作者得出结论,对于28天以下且患有尿路感染(UTI)且严重感染风险因素较低的新生儿,短期静脉抗生素治疗后口服治疗似乎是安全且有效的。这一发现支持了对该年龄段儿童抗生素疗程采取更加个体化的方法。
analysis_zh.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: 这些发现表明,针对新生儿尿路感染(UTI)患者采用更个性化的抗生素疗程可能减少不必要的 治疗,从而改善抗生素使用管理并降低医疗成本。
analysis_zh.limitations_and_evidence_strength: 该研究为回顾性单中心研究,这可能限制其普遍适用性。证据为中等,因为研究结果基于观察性数据,需要前瞻性多中心验证。

papers.title: From Evidence to Implementation: The Added Value of Health Economics for RSV Immunisation Implementation in Low- and Middle-Income Countries
papers.abstract: Respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) is a leading cause of acute lower respiratory infections in young children. In 2019, RSV was estimated to cause approximately 33 million acute lower respiratory infections, 3.6 million hospitalisations and more than 101,000 deaths among children under five years of age, with more than 97% of deaths occurring in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs). The recent availability of a maternal RSV vaccine and long-acting monoclonal antibodies (mAbs) provides new opportunities to prevent severe disease during early infancy. This thesis investigates how epidemiological and health economic evidence can support the implementation of RSV immunisation strategies, with particular emphasis on LMICs. Epidemiological studies first examined RSV burden, seasonality and the age distribution of severe disease. In the Netherlands, RSV circulation was substantially disrupted during the COVID-19 pandemic, including an unusual summer epidemic in 2021, but subsequently returned towards its pre-pandemic winter pattern. Severe disease remained concentrated in young infants. Importantly, 6% of RSV-related hospitalisations among infants aged <1 year occurred within the first 14 days of life, highlighting the importance of timely protection after birth. The RSV GOLD III–ICU Network Study subsequently investigated severe respiratory infections among children aged <2 years across ten LMICs. During local RSV seasons, 29.0% of children admitted with severe respiratory illness tested positive for RSV. Most life-threatening RSV infections occurred among infants aged <6 months, with almost half occurring during the first three months of life, demonstrating the potential for early-life immunisation to prevent severe disease. Cost-of-illness studies in Mozambique and Nepal demonstrated that RSV also imposes a substantial economic burden. In Mozambique, mean costs increased from USD 612 for severe hospitalised disease to USD 1,161 for life-threatening disease requiring intensive care. Household costs represented approximately 43–145% of the monthly minimum wage. In Nepal, mean total costs were USD 312 for hospitalised cases and USD 664 for intensive-care cases, with substantial out-of-pocket expenditure relative to the monthly minimum wage. Cost-effectiveness analyses evaluated maternal vaccination and long-acting mAbs over 2025–2034. In Nepal, maternal vaccination at USD 5 per dose was estimated to prevent approximately 2,500 deaths and 50,000 hospitalisations, with an incremental cost-effectiveness ratio of USD 387 per disability-adjusted life year (DALY) averted. A mAb at the same price could prevent approximately 2,400 deaths and 54,000 hospitalisations at USD 486 per DALY averted. Seasonal delivery could further improve dose efficiency. Analyses in Mozambique similarly demonstrated substantial potential health gains, although cost-effectiveness remained strongly dependent on intervention price and the cost-effectiveness threshold used. Overall, this thesis demonstrates that new RSV immunisation strategies could substantially reduce clinical and economic burden, but their value and feasibility are context-dependent. Integrating local epidemiology, healthcare utilisation, costs and implementation characteristics into economic evaluations can make estimates more relevant for national decision-making. Health economic evidence can thereby support priority setting and resource allocation, while successful and equitable implementation ultimately also depends on affordable pricing, sustainable financing and health-system readiness.

analysis.research_question_and_background: Respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) is a leading cause of acute lower respiratory infections in young children. This thesis investigates how epidemiological and health economic evidence can support the implementation of RSV immunisation strategies, with particular emphasis on low- and middle-income countries (LMICs).
analysis.study_design_and_population: The study examined RSV burden, seasonality, and the age distribution of severe disease in infants. It also included a multinational study across ten LMICs to assess severe respiratory infections in children under two years of age.
analysis.methods: Epidemiological studies were conducted to examine RSV burden, seasonality, and age distribution of severe disease. Cost-of-illness studies and cost-effectiveness analyses were performed in Mozambique and Nepal to evaluate the economic impact and feasibility of immunisation strategies.
analysis.main_results: In the Netherlands, RSV circulation was disrupted during the COVID-19 pandemic, with an unusual summer epidemic in 2021. In ten LMICs, 29.0% of children admitted with severe respiratory illness tested positive for RSV. Cost-of-illness studies in Mozambique and Nepal showed substantial economic burden, with mean costs increasing from USD 612 for severe hospitalised disease to USD 1,161 for life-threatening disease requiring intensive care.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The findings highlight the potential for early-life immunisation to prevent severe disease, as most life-threatening RSV infections occurred among infants under six months of age. The study demonstrates that integrating local epidemiology and economic data can improve the relevance of health economic evaluations for national decision-making.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: Health economic evidence can support priority setting and resource allocation for RSV immunisation strategies in LMICs. The results underscore the importance of affordable pricing, sustainable financing, and health-system readiness for successful implementation.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study is based on abstract-only evidence, which may limit the depth of analysis. The cost-effectiveness of interventions is strongly dependent on price and threshold, and the generalisability of findings may be limited by the specific contexts of the countries studied.

analysis.summary_en: This thesis explores the role of health economics in supporting the implementation of RSV immunisation strategies, particularly in low- and middle-income countries. It highlights the substantial burden of RSV in young children, with severe disease concentrated in infants under six months. Cost-of-illness studies in Mozambique and Nepal reveal significant economic impacts, while cost-effectiveness analyses suggest that maternal vaccination and monoclonal antibodies could prevent thousands of deaths and hospitalisations. The study underscores the importance of integrating local epidemiological and economic data into health evaluations to inform national decision-making. However, the findings are based on abstract-only evidence, and the cost-effectiveness of interventions depends on pricing and thresholds, which may limit their generalisability.

elements_zh.research_question_and_background: 呼吸道合胞病毒(RSV)是导致婴幼儿急性下呼吸道感染的主要原因之一。本论文探讨了流行病学和健康经济学证据如何支持RSV免疫策略的实施,特别强调了低收入和中等收入国家(LMICs)的情况。
elements_zh.study_design_and_population: 本研究评估了婴儿中RSV的负担、季节性和严重疾病的年龄分布。它还包括一项跨国研究,覆盖十个LMICs,以评估<2岁儿童的严重呼吸道感染情况。
elements_zh.methods: 进行了流行病学研究以评估RSV的负担、季节性和严重疾病的年龄分布。在莫桑比克和尼泊尔进行了成本-疾病研究和成本效益分析,以评估免疫策略的经济影响和可行性。
elements_zh.main_results: In the Netherlands, RSV circulation was disrupted during the COVID-19 pandemic, with an unusual summer epidemic in 2021. In ten LMICs, 29.0% of children admitted with severe respiratory illness tested positive for RSV. analysis_en.research_question_and_background: Respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) is a leading cause of acute lower respiratory infections in young children. This thesis investigates how epidemiological and health economic evidence can support the implementation of RSV immunisation strategies, with particular emphasis on low- and middle-income countries (LMICs).
analysis_en.study_design_and_population: The study examined RSV burden, seasonality, and the age distribution of severe disease in infants. It also included a multinational study across ten LMICs to assess severe respiratory infections in children under two years of age.
analysis_en.methods: Epidemiological studies were conducted to examine RSV burden, seasonality, and age distribution of severe disease. Cost-of-illness studies and cost-effectiveness analyses were performed in Mozambique and Nepal to evaluate the economic impact and feasibility of immunisation strategies.
analysis_en.main_results: In the Netherlands, RSV circulation was disrupted during the COVID-19 pandemic, with an unusual summer epidemic in 2021. In ten LMICs, 29.0% of children admitted with severe respiratory illness tested positive for RSV. Cost-of-illness studies in Mozambique and Nepal showed substantial economic burden, with mean costs increasing from USD 612 for severe hospitalised disease to USD 1,161 for life-threatening disease requiring intensive care.
analysis_en.interpretation_and_novelty: The findings highlight the potential for early-life immunisation to prevent severe disease, as most life-threatening RSV infections occurred among infants under six months of age. The study demonstrates that integrating local epidemiology and economic data can improve the relevance of health economic evaluations for national decision-making.
analysis_en.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: Health economic evidence can support priority setting and resource allocation for RSV immunisation strategies in LMICs. The results underscore the importance of affordable pricing, sustainable financing, and health-system readiness for successful implementation.
analysis_en.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study is based on abstract-only evidence, which may limit the depth of analysis. The cost-effectiveness of interventions is strongly dependent on price and threshold, and the generalisability of findings may be limited by the specific contexts of the countries studied.

papers.title_zh: 从证据到实施:健康经济学在低收入和中等收入国家呼吸道合胞病毒免疫实施中的附加价值
papers.source_body_en: Respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) is a leading cause of acute lower respiratory infections in young children. In 2019, RSV was estimated to cause approximately 33 million acute lower respiratory infections, 3.6 million hospitalisations and more than 101,000 deaths among children under five years of age, with more than 97% of deaths occurring in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs). The recent availability of a maternal RSV vaccine and long-acting monoclonal antibodies (mAbs) provides new opportunities to prevent severe disease during early infancy. This thesis investigates how epidemiological and health economic evidence can support the implementation of RSV immunisation strategies, with particular emphasis on LMICs. Epidemiological studies first examined RSV burden, seasonality and the age distribution of severe disease. In the Netherlands, RSV circulation was substantially disrupted during the COVID-19 pandemic, including an unusual summer epidemic in 2021, but subsequently returned towards its pre-pandemic winter pattern. Severe disease remained concentrated in young infants. Importantly, 6% of RSV-related hospitalisations among infants aged <1 year occurred within the first 14 days of life, highlighting the importance of timely protection after birth. The RSV GOLD III–ICU Network Study subsequently investigated severe respiratory infections among children aged <2 years across ten LMICs. During local RSV seasons, 29.0% of children admitted with severe respiratory illness tested positive for RSV. Most life-threatening RSV infections occurred among infants aged <6 months, with almost half occurring during the first three months of life, demonstrating the potential for early-life immunisation to prevent severe disease. Cost-of-illness studies in Mozambique and Nepal demonstrated that RSV also imposes a substantial economic burden. In Mozambique, mean costs increased from USD 612 for severe hospitalised disease to USD 1,161 for life-threatening disease requiring intensive care. Household costs represented approximately 43–145% of the monthly minimum wage. In Nepal, mean total costs were USD 312 for hospitalised cases and USD 664 for intensive-care cases, with substantial out-of-pocket expenditure relative to the monthly minimum wage. Cost-effectiveness analyses evaluated maternal vaccination and long-acting mAbs over 2025–2034. In Nepal, maternal vaccination at USD 5 per dose was estimated to prevent approximately 2,500 deaths and 50,000 hospitalisations, with an incremental cost-effectiveness ratio of USD 387 per disability-adjusted life year (DALY) averted. A mAb at the same price could prevent approximately 2,400 deaths and 54,000 hospitalisations at USD 486 per DALY averted. Seasonal delivery could further improve dose efficiency. Analyses in Mozambique similarly demonstrated substantial potential health gains, although cost-effectiveness remained strongly dependent on intervention price and the cost-effectiveness threshold used. Overall, this thesis demonstrates that new RSV immunisation strategies could substantially reduce clinical and economic burden, but their value and feasibility are context-dependent. Integrating local epidemiology, healthcare utilisation, costs and implementation characteristics into economic evaluations can make estimates more relevant for national decision-making. Health economic evidence can thereby support priority setting and resource allocation, while successful and equitable implementation ultimately also depends on affordable pricing, sustainable financing and health-system readiness.

papers.full_text: ABSTRACTHerpes zoster (HZ) causes substantial morbidity, yet global uptake remains suboptimal where the vaccine is excluded from universal coverage. Taiwan exemplifies such a self-payment setting, with the HZ vaccine self-financed and local government subsidies restricted to limited eligible groups. This study analyzed data from a nationwide, web-based cross-sectional survey of adults aged ≥18y fielded in 2025, examining factors associated with HZ vaccination behavior, intention, and willingness to pay (WTP). Of 1690 respondents, 281 (16.6%) were vaccinated; among 1409 unvaccinated, 1140 (80.9%) were willing to vaccinate. Factors associated with HZ vaccination included age ≥65y (OR: 1.59; 95% CI: 1.12–2.25), prior HZ infection (OR: 1.62; 1.23–2.15), prior receipt of influenza, pneumococcal, or respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) vaccines (OR: 3.32; 2.26–4.89), and awareness of local subsidy programs (OR: 2.30; 1.70–3.12). Among unvaccinated respondents, intention was most strongly associated with high concern about HZ (OR: 3.62; 2.67–4.90). When each prior vaccine was examined separately, prior receipt of self-paid RSV (OR: 5.35; 3.44–8.31) and pneumococcal vaccines (OR: 3.48; 2.54–4.75) showed stronger associations with HZ vaccination than coronavirus disease 2019 (OR: 1.50; 1.04–2.16) or influenza vaccines (OR: 1.51; 1.13–2.02). The median WTP rose stepwise across vaccination statuses (unvaccinated-unwilling: USD 8.2, unvaccinated-willing: USD 32.8, vaccinated: USD 65.6; p < .001), yet all values remained below the market price. In this self-payment setting, HZ vaccination was constrained by affordability rather than lack of motivation. Expanding coverage will require policy action on cost, while prior receipt of self-paid adult vaccines offers a clinically identifiable marker for targeted counseling. MethodsStudy design and respondentsThis study is an analysis of a dataset from the 2025 National Survey on Herpes Zoster Knowledge and Vaccination Attitudes, a nationwide survey commissioned by the Taiwan Association of Family Medicine as a public-opinion poll. The survey was conducted from August 20 to September 2, 2025, by an independent professional survey research organization among adults aged 18 y and older. Participants were recruited through active digital distribution across various online platforms, including e-mails, websites, social media, and search engines. To ensure a representative sample, stratified random sampling was performed based on sex, age, and residential area. This recruitment methodology was widely validated and utilized in recent large-scale epidemiological web surveys.24,25 To prevent duplicate responses and ensure the uniqueness of each participant, digital behavioral profiling and user tagging techniques were integrated into the data collection process. Self-reported demographic information was cross-verified using digital behavioral data matching to ensure data accuracy and reliability.26 Participation in the parent survey was voluntary; respondents were informed of its purpose and agreed to participate before answering the questionnaire, and the survey collected no personally identifiable information. The present analysis of this existing dataset was approved by the Institutional Review Board of National Cheng Kung University Hospital before any analysis was undertaken, with a waiver of informed consent (No. B-ER-115–034, April 2, 2026). This study was conducted in accordance with the principles of the Declaration of Helsinki.Questionnaire surveyThe survey instrument was developed for the parent survey by an expert panel convened by the Taiwan Association of Family Medicine. It was adapted from two previously published studies27,28 and further refined through expert consensus. Each item was reviewed for relevance, accuracy, and clarity by a multidisciplinary panel of specialists in family medicine, geriatrics, and preventive medicine. The panel review established content validity and confirmed cultural and linguistic appropriateness for the Taiwanese setting. Because the instrument used single-item behavioral, attitudinal, and economic measures rather than multi-item latent-construct scales, content validity rather than internal consistency was the appropriate validation standard. The final instrument consisted of 15 items in five sections: (1) demographics and medical history; (2) disease knowledge and risk perception; (3) HZ vaccination behavior, intention, and barriers; (4) prior adult vaccination history; and (5) awareness of local subsidy programs and WTP. Items were presented in true/false, multiple-choice, and 10-point numeric rating scale formats. The questionnaire was developed in Chinese. Demographics and medical history: This section recorded respondents’ sex, age, and residential area (covering 22 administrative divisions in Taiwan). Clinical health status was assessed based on 10 chronic conditions, including diabetes, hypertension, cardiovascular diseases, stroke, chronic respiratory diseases, chronic kidney disease, liver cirrhosis, malignancy, other immunocompromising conditions, and the use of immunosuppressive therapies. These conditions were combined into a single composite indicator owing to sparse individual categories. Personal history of HZ was also documented.Disease knowledge and risk perception: Knowledge of HZ was assessed based on four key clinical facts: high lifetime incidence, high-risk populations, potential for recurrence, and its association with a history of chickenpox. Respondents used 1–10 point scales to rate the perceived pain severity of HZ (1: not painful to 10: most severe pain), its perceived impact on daily life (1: no impact to 10: total disruption), and their level of concern about HZ (1: not concerned to 10: extremely concerned). Because only a minority of respondents had personally experienced HZ, these items were framed as perceptions: respondents with a prior episode answered from personal experience, and those without answered on the basis of their existing knowledge or impression of the disease.HZ vaccination behavior, intention, and barriers: HZ vaccination status was assessed for all individuals. Unvaccinated individuals were further queried regarding their future intention to receive the vaccine. Accordingly, respondents were categorized as (1) vaccinated individuals, (2) unvaccinated individuals willing to be vaccinated (“unvaccinated-willing”), and (3) unvaccinated individuals unwilling to be vaccinated (“unvaccinated-unwilling”). From a list of 10 predefined barriers, unvaccinated participants identified their reasons for not being vaccinated, with multiple selections permitted.Prior adult vaccination history: A history of other adult vaccinations was collected for four vaccines: COVID-19, influenza, pneumococcal, and RSV. These vaccines differ in their funding status in Taiwan. COVID-19 vaccines have been publicly funded for all adults, and influenza vaccines have been publicly funded for adults aged ≥50 y and other priority groups (e.g., healthcare workers, patients with chronic medical illness). The pneumococcal vaccine was self-financed for most adults until October 2023, when public funding was extended to adults aged ≥65 y and high-risk groups. The RSV vaccine, introduced in Taiwan in 2024, has remained entirely self-paid.Awareness of local subsidy programs and willingness to pay: Respondents were asked about their awareness of the localized and conditional HZ vaccine subsidy programs offered by selected local governments in Taiwan. WTP was assessed via an open-ended question, in which participants reported the maximum amount they were willing to pay out-of-pocket for the HZ vaccine. Values were collected in New Taiwan Dollars (TWD) and converted to US Dollars (USD) using the average exchange rate during the survey period (30.5 TWD = 1 USD).Statistical analysisDescriptive statistics are presented as counts and percentages. Comparisons across groups were conducted using χ2 tests. Clinical health status was dichotomized based on the diagnosis of at least one of 10 chronic conditions. Perception scales (pain severity, impact on daily life, and concern level) were rated on 1–10 numeric rating scales and dichotomized into low (1–6) and high (7–10) groups, consistent with the commonly used cutoff of ≥7 to denote a high level on numeric rating scales.Multivariable logistic regression models were employed to identify independent factors associated with two primary outcomes: (1) HZ vaccination behavior (vaccinated vs. unvaccinated) among the total population, and (2) HZ vaccination intention (willing vs. unwilling) among unvaccinated individuals. These models were adjusted for sex, age, chronic medical illness, history of HZ, concern level regarding HZ, and awareness of local subsidy programs. Six logistic regression models were constructed for each primary outcome, each containing a different prior vaccination variable. This approach evaluated the influence of prior immunization at multiple levels while avoiding multicollinearity. Models 1 to 4 examined the influence of each individual prior vaccine separately, with prior receipt of COVID-19 vaccine (Model 1), influenza vaccine (Model 2), pneumococcal vaccine (Model 3), and RSV vaccine (Model 4) as the predictors of interest. Models 5 and 6 used composite measures. Model 5 served as the primary composite analysis, examining prior receipt of any non-COVID-19 adult vaccine (influenza, pneumococcal, or RSV); this composite was designed to isolate the influence of vaccinations requiring more active health-seeking behavior, given that the near-universal COVID-19 vaccination coverage in Taiwan would otherwise obscure such associations. Model 6 was conducted as a sensitivity analysis, examining prior receipt of any adult vaccine (COVID-19, influenza, pneumococcal, or RSV), to assess whether the composite findings remained robust when the universally funded COVID-19 vaccine was included. As a further sensitivity analysis, the primary multivariable models were repeated with the sample restricted to respondents aged ≥50 y, the principal target age for HZ vaccination.For the WTP analysis, cumulative distribution curves were generated to visualize the maximum out-of-pocket amounts participants were willing to pay, an approach adopted from previous vaccine WTP studies.29,30 For comparisons among three groups stratified by HZ vaccination behavior and intention (vaccinated, unvaccinated-willing, and unvaccinated-unwilling), the Kruskal‒Wallis test was used, followed by Dunn’s post-hoc test with Bonferroni correction for pairwise comparisons. For comparisons between two groups stratified by history of other non-COVID-19 adult vaccinations (yes vs. no), the Mann‒Whitney U test was used. Effect sizes were reported as eta-squared (η2) for Kruskal‒Wallis and r (|Z|/√N) for Mann‒Whitney U tests.All analyses were performed using IBM SPSS Statistics (version 27.0; IBM Corp., Armonk, NY, USA). A p value less than .05 was considered statistically significant. full_text_sections.abstract: ABSTRACTHerpes zoster (HZ) causes substantial morbidity, yet global uptake remains suboptimal where the vaccine is excluded from universal coverage. Taiwan exemplifies such a self-payment setting, with the HZ vaccine self-financed and local government subsidies restricted to limited eligible groups. This study analyzed data from a nationwide, web-based cross-sectional survey of adults aged ≥18y fielded in 2025, examining factors associated with HZ vaccination behavior, intention, and willingness to pay (WTP). Of 1690 respondents, 281 (16.6%) were vaccinated; among 1409 unvaccinated, 1140 (80.9%) were willing to vaccinate. Factors associated with HZ vaccination included age ≥65y (OR: 1.59; 95% CI: 1.12–2.25), prior HZ infection (OR: 1.62; 1.23–2.15), prior receipt of influenza, pneumococcal, or respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) vaccines (OR: 3.32; 2.26–4.89), and awareness of local subsidy programs (OR: 2.30; 1.70–3.12). Among unvaccinated respondents, intention was most strongly associated with high concern about HZ (OR: 3.62; 2.67–4.90). When each prior vaccine was examined separately, prior receipt of self-paid RSV (OR: 5.35; 3.44–8.31) and pneumococcal vaccines (OR: 3.48; 2.54–4.75) showed stronger associations with HZ vaccination than coronavirus disease 2019 (OR: 1.50; 1.04–2.16) or influenza vaccines (OR: 1.51; 1.13–2.02). The median WTP rose stepwise across vaccination statuses (unvaccinated-unwilling: USD 8.2, unvaccinated-willing: USD 32.8, vaccinated: USD 65.6; p < .001), yet all values remained below the market price. In this self-payment setting, HZ vaccination was constrained by affordability rather than lack of motivation. Expanding coverage will require policy action on cost, while prior receipt of self-paid adult vaccines offers a clinically identifiable marker for targeted counseling.

full_text_sections.discussion: DiscussionIn this nationwide cross-sectional survey of adults examining HZ vaccination behavior and intention in a predominantly self-payment setting, four principal findings emerged. First, vaccination intention substantially exceeded actual uptake, indicating a pronounced intention–behavior gap. Second, the correlates of intention and behavior diverged: concern about HZ was associated with intention only, and a prior HZ episode with behavior only. Third, prior receipt of self-paid adult vaccines showed the strongest association with vaccination behavior. Fourth, the public’s WTP fell well below the market price of HZ vaccine and was lowest among individuals with lower vaccine acceptance. Together, these findings indicate that intention and behavior are associated with distinct factors, a pattern consistent with motivational factors relating to intention and economic factors relating to uptake.In this self-payment setting, HZ vaccination coverage and intention were comparable to or higher than most international reports, yet this favorable engagement did not translate proportionally into actual uptake. The HZ vaccination coverage in this study was 21.0% among adults aged ≥50 y and 26.2% among those aged ≥65 y. This exceeds the coverage rates reported in China (0.79% among those aged ≥40 y in 2024)16 and the United States (17% among those aged ≥50 y in 2021)13 but remains lower than in Australia (32% among those aged ≥65 y in 2019–2020).15 Notably, four in five unvaccinated respondents (1140 of 1409, 80.9%) were willing to vaccinate, substantially exceeding the 55.74% pooled global willingness rate reported in a 2023 systematic review and meta-analysis.31 The contrast between this strong vaccination intention and the suboptimal actual coverage indicates that public attitude is unlikely to be the primary obstacle. Rather, a substantive intention–behavior gap separates the willing from the vaccinated.Concern level regarding HZ was the factor most strongly associated with vaccination intention but was not associated with actual behavior. Among the unvaccinated respondents, those with high concern levels had more than three times the odds of expressing willingness to vaccinate (OR: 3.62; 95% CI: 2.67–4.90). However, concern level was not independently associated with actual HZ vaccination. This discrepancy suggests that while concern accompanies the intention to be immunized, concern alone appears insufficient to translate intention into actual vaccination under self-payment conditions. Whereas multiple cross-sectional studies have demonstrated that higher perceived risk is associated with greater willingness to receive the HZ vaccine,32–35 our analysis extends these findings by showing that this motivational pathway does not appear to translate into actual uptake when cost remains a barrier.Conversely, a prior HZ infection was associated with actual vaccination but not with future intention among unvaccinated individuals. Stated differently, among those who had experienced HZ but remained unvaccinated, prior infection was not associated with willingness to vaccinate. This null association can be explained by the pattern of self-reported reasons for non-vaccination shown in Figure 1. Among unvaccinated respondents, “perceived lack of need due to prior HZ history” was cited as a barrier more than three times as often by the unwilling group than the willing group (18.6% vs. 5.9%, p < .001; Figure 1). This suggests that a substantial proportion of people with prior HZ believe a single episode confers lasting protection and therefore see no reason to vaccinate. This belief, however, overlooks the well-documented potential for HZ recurrence, and current Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices (ACIP) guidelines explicitly recommend HZ vaccination irrespective of prior HZ history.9,36,37 Public education should be targeted rather than generic. Adults with a prior HZ episode are identifiable in routine practice and remain at risk of recurrence, and counseling at diagnosis or subsequent visits could address recurrence risk, post-episode vaccine efficacy, and the related misconceptions of low susceptibility and severity.Whereas prior HZ history reflects direct disease experience, prior receipt of other adult vaccinations represents a different behavioral pathway – one that emerged as an even stronger predictor of HZ vaccination uptake. A history of other non-COVID-19 adult vaccinations was the strongest predictor of HZ vaccination behavior and an independent predictor of intention. The vaccine-specific findings revealed a clear gradient by funding mechanism of each prior vaccine. The entirely self-paid RSV vaccine showed the strongest association (Model 4, OR: 5.35), followed by the recently transitioned pneumococcal vaccine (Model 3, OR: 3.48), and then the long-publicly-funded influenza and COVID-19 vaccines (Models 2 and 1: OR: 1.51 and 1.50, respectively). This gradient suggests that the association reflects individuals’ out-of-pocket spending on preventive care rather than vaccination habits per se. To our knowledge, this is the first study to demonstrate a funding-mechanism gradient in prior vaccination as a predictor of HZ vaccine uptake, providing a novel framework for understanding vaccination decisions in self-payment settings.Clinical risk groups warrant separate consideration. Diabetes is associated with an approximately 40% increase in HZ incidence.38,39 Immunocompromising conditions and immunosuppressive therapies raise the risk of HZ, postherpetic neuralgia, disseminated disease, and HZ-related hospitalization.40 ACIP therefore recommends RZV for immunodeficient or immunosuppressed adults from age 19.9 Nonetheless, chronic medical illness was not associated with vaccination behavior or intention. This null association persisted across all six regression models (Tables 2 and 3) and in the analysis restricted to adults aged ≥50 y (Supplementary Table 1). Elevated clinical risk therefore did not distinguish those who vaccinated from those who did not. This finding should be interpreted with caution. Individual conditions were too sparse for stable estimation and were analyzed as a single composite indicator. This indicator grouped severely immunosuppressed patients with those having more common conditions, and such aggregation may have diluted a genuine association among the most immunocompromised. Even so, the absence of any signal suggests that clinical risk is not currently a principal driver of vaccination in this self-payment setting. Clinician-initiated counseling could address this gap.Across these findings, affordability emerged as the central obstacle separating intention from behavior, and our data build a cumulative case for this conclusion through two lines of evidence. First, cost was the most frequently cited barrier in both unvaccinated subgroups and was cited more often by the willing group than by the unwilling group (62.1% vs. 40.9%, p < .001; Figure 1). This pattern is consistent with prior literature identifying high vaccine cost as the primary barrier to HZ vaccination28,33,41,42 and indicates that cost is the proximal obstacle particularly for those who would otherwise vaccinate. Second, our WTP analysis provides direct quantitative evidence that financial constraints are not merely perceived but objectively present, and that this constraint scales with vaccine acceptance. Figure 2(A) reveals a stepwise WTP gradient across groups defined by HZ vaccination behavior and intention (vaccinated USD 65.6 > unvaccinated-willing USD 32.8 > unvaccinated-unwilling USD 8.2; all pairwise p < .001). Figure 2(B) also shows a parallel pattern when respondents were stratified by history of other non-COVID-19 adult vaccinations (with vs. without history: USD 32.8 vs. USD 16.4, p < .001). Together, these analyses demonstrate that individuals with lower vaccine acceptance – whether defined by HZ behavior and intention or by prior adult vacci…
full_text_sections.conclusion: ConclusionIn this self-payment setting, lower HZ vaccination uptake was associated more with cost barriers than with a lack of motivation. Measured WTP fell substantially below the market price of RZV. Concern about HZ was associated with vaccination intention; however, this association alone did not appear sufficient to close the intention–behavior gap. These findings suggest that expanding coverage will likely require policy action on cost. In parallel, prior receipt of self-paid adult vaccines may offer a clinically identifiable marker for targeting counseling and co-administration efforts.
full_text_sections.other: IntroductionHerpes zoster (HZ), the clinical reactivation of latent varicella-zoster virus, affects approximately one in three persons during their lifetime, with the highest burden among older adults.1–4 Acute herpetic neuralgia and postherpetic neuralgia (PHN) – the most common long-term complication – substantially impair quality of life and functional independence.5 Beyond the established age-related risk, recent evidence indicates that prior coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19) infection further increases the one-year risk of HZ (hazard ratios, 1.59 to 2.16), broadening the population at risk.6,7Two efficacious vaccines are available for primary prevention. The live attenuated zoster vaccine reduces the incidence of HZ and PHN by 67% and 83% in the first year following administration.8 The recombinant zoster vaccine (RZV), now the preferred option in most national programs,9 reduces the risk of HZ and PHN by 97.2% and 91.2%, respectively, with a complete two-dose regimen.10 Despite this efficacy, global uptake remains suboptimal,11–13 in part because HZ vaccination is excluded from universal national health coverage in many countries and remains primarily an out-of-pocket expense.14 Uptake varies markedly by funding mechanism. Coverage reaches approximately one-third of eligible older adults where HZ vaccination is publicly funded and nationally recommended (32% among adults aged ≥65 y in Australia15), but is substantially lower where the vaccine remains an out-of-pocket expense (0.79% among adults aged ≥40 y in China16). This contrast underscores the value of examining the determinants of uptake specifically under self-payment conditions, where the decision to vaccinate is also a decision to pay.Taiwan provides an instructive case of such a self-payment setting, where the HZ vaccine is predominantly funded out-of-pocket rather than through universal coverage. The HZ vaccine is not included in Taiwan’s National Health Insurance program or the national immunization schedule. Although some local governments offer partial subsidies, eligibility is mostly restricted to economically disadvantaged individuals, leaving most adults to pay the full cost out-of-pocket. Understanding what drives vaccination uptake under such self-payment conditions is therefore relevant not only to Taiwan but also to the many regions where comprehensive public funding has yet to be established. Behavioral theory anticipates that motivation alone may not suffice in such settings. Both the Health Belief Model and the 5C framework of vaccination psychology treat cost as a structural barrier capable of overriding favorable attitudes,17–20 and the resulting intention–behavior gap is well documented across health behaviors.21 We therefore analyzed vaccination intention and behavior as separate outcomes.Two questions central to expanding HZ vaccination coverage in a self-payment setting remain inadequately addressed. First, it is unclear whether adults who have received other vaccines are more likely to receive the HZ vaccine. Prior vaccination behavior may reflect general health-seeking tendencies, vaccine confidence, or regular healthcare contact, which can predict future vaccination decisions.22,23 It is also unknown whether this association differs depending on whether the prior vaccine was publicly funded or paid out-of-pocket. Adults who have already paid out-of-pocket for one vaccine may be more willing to do so for additional self-paid vaccines such as HZ, but this hypothesis has not been tested. Second, the determinants of willingness to pay (WTP) for the HZ vaccine remain poorly understood, particularly whether WTP is influenced by vaccination behavior, intention, and prior adult vaccination history.To address these gaps and to provide insights applicable to similar self-payment settings worldwide, we analyzed data from a nationwide, web-based cross-sectional survey of adults in Taiwan, with the aim of identifying what separates the intention to vaccinate from the act of vaccinating when the cost is borne by the individual. Specifically, we aimed to (1) determine the prevalence of HZ vaccination and the intention to vaccinate among unvaccinated adults; (2) identify factors independently associated with vaccination behavior and intention, with particular focus on the influence of prior adult vaccination history; and (3) assess WTP for the HZ vaccine, including its variation by vaccination behavior, intention, and prior adult vaccination history. Questionnaire surveyThe survey instrument was developed for the parent survey by an expert panel convened by the Taiwan Association of Family Medicine. It was adapted from two previously published studies27,28 and further refined through expert consensus. Each item was reviewed for relevance, accuracy, and clarity by a multidisciplinary panel of specialists in family medicine, geriatrics, and preventive medicine. The panel review established content validity and confirmed cultural and linguistic appropriateness for the Taiwanese setting. Because the instrument used single-item behavioral, attitudinal, and economic measures rather than multi-item latent-construct scales, content validity rather than internal consistency was the appropriate validation standard. The final instrument consisted of 15 items in five sections: (1) demographics and medical history; (2) disease knowledge and risk perception; (3) HZ vaccination behavior, intention, and barriers; (4) prior adult vaccination history; and (5) awareness of local subsidy programs and WTP. Items were presented in true/false, multiple-choice, and 10-point numeric rating scale formats. The questionnaire was developed in Chinese. Demographics and medical history: This section recorded respondents’ sex, age, and residential area (covering 22 administrative divisions in Taiwan). Clinical health status was assessed based on 10 chronic conditions, including diabetes, hypertension, cardiovascular diseases, stroke, chronic respiratory diseases, chronic kidney disease, liver cirrhosis, malignancy, other immunocompromising conditions, and the use of immunosuppressive therapies. These conditions were combined into a single composite indicator owing to sparse individual categories. Personal history of HZ was also documented.Disease knowledge and risk perception: Knowledge of HZ was assessed based on four key clinical facts: high lifetime incidence, high-risk populations, potential for recurrence, and its association with a history of chickenpox. Respondents used 1–10 point scales to rate the perceived pain severity of HZ (1: not painful to 10: most severe pain), its perceived impact on daily life (1: no impact to 10: total disruption), and their level of concern about HZ (1: not concerned to 10: extremely concerned). Because only a minority of respondents had personally experienced HZ, these items were framed as perceptions: respondents with a prior episode answered from personal experience, and those without answered on the basis of their existing knowledge or impression of the disease.HZ vaccination behavior, intention, and barriers: HZ vaccination status was assessed for all individuals. Unvaccinated individuals were further queried regarding their future intention to receive the vaccine. Accordingly, respondents were categorized as (1) vaccinated individuals, (2) unvaccinated individuals willing to be vaccinated (“unvaccinated-willing”), and (3) unvaccinated individuals unwilling to be vaccinated (“unvaccinated-unwilling”). From a list of 10 predefined barriers, unvaccinated participants identified their reasons for not being vaccinated, with multiple selections permitted.Prior adult vaccination history: A history of other adult vaccinations was collected for four vaccines: COVID-19, influenza, pneumococcal, and RSV. analysis.research_question_and_background: This study aimed to understand factors influencing herpes zoster (HZ) vaccination behavior and intention in a self-payment setting, addressing the gap in knowledge about how affordability and motivation interact in vaccine uptake.
analysis.study_design_and_population: A nationwide, web-based cross-sectional survey of adults aged ≥18 years was conducted in 2025, with participants recruited through active digital distribution across online platforms. The sample included 1690 respondents categorized into three groups based on their HZ vaccination status.
analysis.methods: Clinical health status was assessed based on 10 chronic conditions, and perceived pain severity, impact on daily life, and concern levels were self-rated on 1–10 numeric scales. Logistic regression models were used to analyze associations between prior vaccination history and HZ vaccination behavior or intention, with six separate models constructed for each outcome.
analysis.main_results: HZ vaccination behavior was significantly associated with age ≥65 years (OR: 1.59; 95% CI: 1.12–2.25), prior HZ infection (OR: 1.62; 95% CI: 1.23–2.15), prior receipt of non-COVID-19 adult vaccines (OR: 3.32; 95% CI: 2.26–4.89), and awareness of local subsidy programs (OR: 2.30; 95% CI: 1.70–3.12).
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The study highlights that prior receipt of non-COVID-19 adult vaccines, particularly RSV and pneumococcal vaccines, is strongly associated with HZ vaccination behavior, suggesting a potential link between health-seeking behaviors and vaccine uptake.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: These findings can inform public health strategies to improve HZ vaccination rates by leveraging existing vaccination behaviors and promoting awareness of subsidy programs to reduce financial barriers.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study is limited by its reliance on self-reported data and the potential for recall bias. However, the use of logistic regression models and sensitivity analyses strengthens the evidence, supporting a moderate confidence assessment.

analysis.summary_en: This study investigated factors influencing herpes zoster (HZ) vaccination behavior and intention in a self-payment setting, focusing on a nationwide survey of 1690 adults. It found that age ≥65 years, prior HZ infection, and prior receipt of non-COVID-19 adult vaccines were significantly associated with HZ vaccination behavior. The study also noted that awareness of local subsidy programs increased the likelihood of vaccination. The median willingness to pay for the HZ vaccine was below the market price, indicating affordability as a barrier. The research highlights the importance of health-seeking behaviors and financial incentives in vaccine uptake, with implications for improving public health strategies. While the study has limitations due to self-reporting, the use of logistic regression models and sensitivity analyses provides moderate confidence in the findings.

analysis_zh.research_question_and_background: 本研究旨在了解在自费环境下,影响水痘带状疱疹病毒(HZ)疫苗接种行为和意图的因素,填补关于可负担性和动机如何相互作用以促进疫苗接种的知识空白。
analysis_zh.study_design_and_population: 2025年进行了一项全国范围的网络横断面调查,调查对象为≥18岁的成年人,通过在线平台的主动数字分发招募参与者。样本包括1690名受访者,根据其HZ 疫苗接种状态分为三组。
analysis_zh.methods: 临床健康状况基于10种慢性疾病进行评估,疼痛感知严重程度、对日常生活的感知影响以及担忧程度均采用1–10的数值量表进行自我评分。使用逻辑回归模型分析既往疫苗接种史与HZ 疫苗接种行为或意图之间的关联,并为每项结果构建了六个独立的模型。
analysis_zh.main_results: HZ 疫苗接种行为与年龄≥65岁(OR:1.59;95% CI:1.12–2.25)、既往HZ感染史(OR:1.62;95% CI:1.23–2.15)、既往接受过非新冠19成人疫苗史(OR:3.32;95% CI:2.26–4.89)以及知晓本地补贴计划(OR:2.30;95% CI:1.70–3.12)显著相关。
analysis_zh.interpretation_and_novelty: 本研究强调,既往接受过非新冠19成人疫苗,特别是呼吸道合胞病毒(RSV)和肺炎球菌疫苗,与HZ 疫苗接种行为有显著关联,这表明健康行为寻求与疫苗接种之间可能存在潜在联系。
analysis_zh.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: 这些发现可以为公共卫生策略提供信息,通过利用现有的疫苗接种行为并促进对补贴计划的认知,以减少经济障碍,提高HZ 疫苗接种接种率。
analysis_zh.limitations_and_evidence_strength: 本研究的局限性在于依赖自我报告数据,可能存在回忆偏差。然而,使用逻辑回归模型和敏感性分析增强了证据的强度,支持中等程度的置信度评估。

source_records.title: The H3K27me3-NR1D1-IFN-γ axis in trained macrophages induced by early respiratory virus infection drives non-T2 asthma in children

papers.priority_tier_reason: 补充性记录、预印本或证据完整度有限
papers.full_text: Abstract Unlike that of T2 asthma, the pathophysiology of non–T2 asthma remains largely unexplored. However, increasing evidence supports a role for trained macrophages in asthma. In this study, we utilized a non-T2 asthma mouse model associated with early respiratory viral infection to identify the H3K27me3-NR1D1-IFN-γ axis in lung-trained macrophages, which drives non-T2 asthma by promoting Th1 differentiation. Early infection combined with allergen sensitization induced the formation of trained macrophages, which displayed hyperactive methionine cycling and elevated levels of S-adenosylmethionine (SAM). As a substrate for methyltransferase, SAM enhanced the trimethylation of H3K27, subsequently suppressing the expression of the nuclear receptor subfamily 1 group D member 1 (NR1D1) gene through enrichment at its promoter. Interestingly, NR1D1 interacted with the Ifng gene and negatively regulated its expression. High levels of IFN-γ from trained macrophages were observed because NR1D1 was inhibited by elevated H3K27me3 levels. Following allergen challenge, the increased expression of IFN-γ, MHC-II, and CD80/CD86 in trained macrophages positively regulated the activation and differentiation of Th1 cells, which subsequently produced more IFN-γ, thereby promoting non-T2 asthma. Consistently, in patients with asthma, peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMCs) and monocytes downregulated NR1D1 expression, resulting in elevated IFN-γ levels. Conversely, treatment of patient monocytes with an NR1D1 agonist led to a marked decrease in IFN-γ production. In mice, non-T2 asthma was significantly inhibited by either the inhibition of H3K27me3, the activation of NR1D1, or the neutralization of IFN-γ. Our results demonstrate that the H3K27me3-NR1D1-IFN-γ axis in lung-trained macrophages, which is associated with early infection, drives non-T2 asthma during childhood in mice. Consequently, SAM, NR1D1, and IFN-γ may serve as potential drug targets for the treatment of non-T2 asthma. full_text_sections.full_text: Abstract Unlike that of T2 asthma, the pathophysiology of non–T2 asthma remains largely unexplored. However, increasing evidence supports a role for trained macrophages in asthma. In this study, we utilized a non-T2 asthma mouse model associated with early respiratory viral infection to identify the H3K27me3-NR1D1-IFN-γ axis in lung-trained macrophages, which drives non-T2 asthma by promoting Th1 differentiation. Early infection combined with allergen sensitization induced the formation of trained macrophages, which displayed hyperactive methionine cycling and elevated levels of S-adenosylmethionine (SAM). As a substrate for methyltransferase, SAM enhanced the trimethylation of H3K27, subsequently suppressing the expression of the nuclear receptor subfamily 1 group D member 1 (NR1D1) gene through enrichment at its promoter. Interestingly, NR1D1 interacted with the Ifng gene and negatively regulated its expression. High levels of IFN-γ from trained macrophages were observed because NR1D1 was inhibited by elevated H3K27me3 levels. Following allergen challenge, the increased expression of IFN-γ, MHC-II, and CD80/CD86 in trained macrophages positively regulated the activation and differentiation of Th1 cells, which subsequently produced more IFN-γ, thereby promoting non-T2 asthma. Consistently, in patients with asthma, peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMCs) and monocytes downregulated NR1D1 expression, resulting in elevated IFN-γ levels. Conversely, treatment of patient monocytes with an NR1D1 agonist led to a marked decrease in IFN-γ production. In mice, non-T2 asthma was significantly inhibited by either the inhibition of H3K27me3, the activation of NR1D1, or the neutralization of IFN-γ. Our results demonstrate that the H3K27me3-NR1D1-IFN-γ axis in lung-trained macrophages, which is associated with early infection, drives non-T2 asthma during childhood in mice. Consequently, SAM, NR1D1, and IFN-γ may serve as potential drug targets for the treatment of non-T2 asthma. papers.title_original: The H3K27me3-NR1D1-IFN-γ axis in trained macrophages induced by early respiratory virus infection drives non-T2 asthma in children

analysis.research_question_and_background: The study aimed to investigate the pathophysiology of non-T2 asthma, which remains largely unexplored, and to identify mechanisms by which early respiratory viral infection contributes to its development.
analysis.study_design_and_population: The study used a non-T2 asthma mouse model induced by early respiratory viral infection combined with allergen sensitization. The model involved trained macrophages that displayed hyperactive methionine cycling and elevated levels of S-adenosylmethionine (SAM).
analysis.methods: The methods included the use of a non-T2 asthma mouse model, allergen challenge, and analysis of gene expression and cytokine levels in trained macrophages. SAM levels were linked to H3K27me3 trimethylation, which was shown to suppress NR1D1 gene expression through promoter enrichment.
analysis.main_results: Following allergen challenge, trained macrophages showed increased expression of IFN-γ, MHC-II, and CD80/CD86, which positively regulated Th1 cell activation and differentiation. In patients with asthma, PBMCs and monocytes downregulated NR1D1 expression, resulting in elevated IFN-γ levels.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The authors interpreted that the H3K27me3-NR1D1-IFN-γ axis in lung-trained macrophages, associated with early infection, drives non-T2 asthma in children, offering a novel mechanistic insight into the development of this asthma subtype.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings suggest that targeting SAM, NR1D1, or IFN-γ could provide therapeutic options for non-T2 asthma, potentially informing future research and treatment strategies for this condition.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study is limited by its reliance on a mouse model and the lack of direct human clinical trials. However, the results are supported by consistent findings in both mice and human asthma patients, providing moderate confidence in the proposed mechanism.

analysis.summary_en: This study explores the pathophysiology of non-T2 asthma, which is less understood compared to T2 asthma. The research focuses on the role of early respiratory viral infection in inducing trained macrophages, which contribute to non-T2 asthma through the H3K27me3-NR1D1-IFN-γ axis. The study demonstrates that SAM enhances H3K27me3 trimethylation, suppressing NR1D1 expression and leading to elevated IFN-γ levels. These findings suggest that the H3K27me3-NR1D1-IFN-γ pathway may be a potential therapeutic target for non-T2 asthma. The results are supported by both in vivo and in vitro evidence, though the study is limited to a mouse model and lacks direct human clinical trials. The implications of the study highlight the importance of understanding the interplay between viral infections and immune responses in childhood asthma.

elements_zh.research_question_and_background: 本研究旨在探讨非T2哮喘的病理生理学机制,该机制仍 largely unexplored,并识别早期呼吸道病毒感染如何促进其发展。
elements_zh.study_design_and_population: 本研究使用了由早期呼吸道病毒感染结合过敏原致敏诱导的非T2哮喘小鼠模型。该模型涉及表现出高活性甲硫氨酸循环和S-腺苷甲硫氨酸(SAM)水平升高的训练型巨噬细胞。
elements_zh.methods: 研究方法包括使用非T2哮喘小鼠模型、过敏原挑战以及对训练型巨噬细胞中基因表达和细胞因子水平的分析。SAM水平与H3K27me3三甲基化相关,该三甲基化通过启动子区域的富集被证明可抑制NR1D1基因的表达。
elements_zh.main_results: 在过敏原挑战后,训练型巨噬细胞表现出IFN-γ、MHC-II和CD80/CD86的表达增加,这些因子正向调控Th1细胞的激活和分化。在哮喘患者中,外周血单核细胞(PBMCs)和单核细胞下调NR1D1表达,导致IFN-γ水平升高。
elements_zh.interpretation_and_novelty: 作者解释认为,与早期感染相关的肺部训练型巨噬细胞中的H3K27me3-NR1D1-IFN-γ轴驱动儿童非T2哮喘,为这一哮喘亚型的发展提供了新的机制见解。
elements_zh.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: 这些发现表明,针对SAM、NR1D1或IFN-γ可能为非T2哮喘提供治疗选择,可能为未来针对该疾病的研究和治疗策略提供信息。
elements_zh.limitations_and_evidence_strength: 本研究的局限性在于其依赖于小鼠模型,并缺乏直接的人类临床试验。然而,研究结果在小鼠和哮喘患者中均表现出一致性,为所提出的机制提供了中等程度的可信度。

analysis_en.research_question_and_background: The study aimed to investigate the pathophysiology of non-T2 asthma, which remains largely unexplored, and to identify mechanisms by which early respiratory viral infection contributes to its development.
analysis_en.study_design_and_population: The study used a non-T2 asthma mouse model induced by early respiratory viral infection combined with allergen sensitization. The model involved trained macrophages that displayed hyperactive methionine cycling and elevated levels of S-adenosylmethionine (SAM).
analysis_en.methods: The methods included the use of a non-T2 asthma mouse model, allergen challenge, and analysis of gene expression and cytokine levels in trained macrophages. SAM levels were linked to H3K27me3 trimethylation, which was shown to suppress NR1D1 gene expression through promoter enrichment.
analysis_en.main_results: Following allergen challenge, trained macrophages showed increased expression of IFN-γ, MHC-II, and CD80/CD86, which positively regulated Th1 cell activation and differentiation. In patients with asthma, PBMCs and monocytes downregulated NR1D1 expression, resulting in elevated IFN-γ levels.
analysis_en.interpretation_and_novelty: The authors interpreted that the H3K27me3-NR1D1-IFN-γ axis in lung-trained macrophages, associated with early infection, drives non-T2 asthma in children, offering a novel mechanistic insight into the development of this asthma subtype.
analysis_en.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings suggest that targeting SAM, NR1D1, or IFN-γ could provide therapeutic options for non-T2 asthma, potentially informing future research and treatment strategies for this condition.
analysis_en.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study is limited by its reliance on a mouse model and the lack of direct human clinical trials. However, the results are supported by consistent findings in both mice and human asthma patients, providing moderate confidence in the proposed mechanism.

papers.source_body_en: In this study, we utilized a non-T2 asthma mouse model associated with early respiratory viral infection to identify the H3K27me3-NR1D1-IFN-γ axis in lung-trained macrophages, which drives non-T2 asthma by promoting Th1 differentiation. Our results demonstrate that the H3K27me3-NR1D1-IFN-γ axis in lung-trained macrophages, which is associated with early infection, drives non-T2 asthma during childhood in mice. A review of epigenetic changes in asthma: methylation and acetylation. Abstract Unlike that of T2 asthma, the pathophysiology of non–T2 asthma remains largely unexplored. However, increasing evidence supports a role for trained macrophages in asthma. Early infection combined with allergen sensitization induced the formation of trained macrophages, which displayed hyperactive methionine cycling and elevated levels of S-adenosylmethionine (SAM). As a substrate for methyltransferase, SAM enhanced the trimethylation of H3K27, subsequently suppressing the expression of the nuclear receptor subfamily 1 group D member 1 (NR1D1) gene through enrichment at its promoter. Interestingly, NR1D1 interacted with the Ifng gene and negatively regulated its expression. High levels of IFN-γ from trained macrophages were observed because NR1D1 was inhibited by elevated H3K27me3 levels. Following allergen challenge, the increased expression of IFN-γ, MHC-II, and CD80/CD86 in trained macrophages positively regulated the activation and differentiation of Th1 cells, which subsequently produced more IFN-γ, thereby promoting non-T2 asthma. Consistently, in patients with asthma, peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMCs) and monocytes downregulated NR1D1 expression, resulting in elevated IFN-γ levels. papers.full_text: IntroductionPost-pandemic re-emergence of Mycoplasma pneumoniae has raised concern about pediatric hospital burden and intensive-care demand. We described temporal trends, age-stratified diagnosis-coded phenotypes, pathogen-related coded co-diagnoses, and variables associated with PICU-associated hospitalization.MethodsWe conducted a single-center retrospective study based on diagnosis-coded discharge records from a tertiary maternal and child health hospital in Hubei, China. Hospitalization records of children aged 29 days to <18 years with finalized diagnosis-coded M. pneumoniae-associated illness from June 2020 to March 2026 were screened; neonatal, adult, and manually verified repeated records were excluded. A stratified chart-validation subset (n = 762) summarized microbiological evidence and selected coding-derived variables.ResultsThe analytic dataset included 33,047 pediatric hospitalization records; 16,848 (51.0%) were male and 872 (2.6%) were PICU-associated. Monthly records peaked in November 2023 (2,282), whereas PICU-associated records and rate peaked in October 2023 (99; 4.95%). Respiratory failure/hypoxemia was recorded in 6.6% of the 1–<12 mo group versus 1.3% of the 72–<144 mo group; coded sepsis/septicemia in 11.2% versus 5.9%; and cardiac abnormality/coded myocardial involvement in 25.0% versus 15.6%. Atelectasis and consolidation peaked in the 72–<144 mo group (24.1 and 13.0%). The most common pathogen-related coded co-diagnoses were respiratory syncytial virus (2,096; 6.3%), rhinovirus (2,031; 6.1%), Haemophilus influenzae (1,351; 4.1%), adenovirus (1,348; 4.1%), and influenza virus (956; 2.9%). In the extended exploratory model, age 1–<12 mo (aOR, 2.59; 95% CI, 2.07–3.24), age 12–<36 mo (aOR, 1.70; 95% CI, 1.40–2.07), influenza virus (aOR, 2.07; 95% CI, 1.50–2.86), respiratory syncytial virus (aOR, 1.83; 95% CI, 1.43–2.35), and major chronic/congenital comorbidity (aOR, 8.07; 95% CI, 6.69–9.74) were associated with PICU-associated hospitalization.ConclusionDiagnosis-coded pediatric M. pneumoniae-associated hospitalization records increased after June 2023 and peaked in November 2023, with age-structured coded phenotype patterns and measurable PICU-associated burden. Findings represent hospital-based diagnosis-coded patterns, not laboratory-adjudicated incident infections or population incidence. 2Methods2.1Study design and data sourceThis retrospective discharge-abstract study used a de-identified structured inpatient discharge dataset from Maternal and Child Health Hospital of Hubei Province. The dataset reflected routine hospital documentation, discharge diagnosis coding, and department-field recording. Because the primary analysis used finalized discharge abstracts rather than full clinical-chart adjudication, all phenotype and pathogen variables derived from discharge diagnosis labels were interpreted as diagnosis-coded variables. Reporting was guided by principles for observational studies using routinely collected health data, including transparency of data source, coding algorithms, and outcome definitions (13–15).2.2Study population and data cleaningThe initial screening dataset contained 34,562 diagnosis-coded M. pneumoniae-associated hospitalization records. Records from children aged <29 days (n = 55), records from patients aged ≥18 years (n = 1,436), and repeated hospitalization records identified through manual verification (n = 24) were excluded. The final analytic dataset included 33,047 eligible pediatric hospitalization records aged ≥29 days and <18 years (Supplementary Figure S1). The unit of analysis was the hospitalization record. Age was calculated at admission and expressed in month-based clinical categories: 1–<12 mo, 12–<36 mo, 36–<72 mo, 72–<144 mo, and 144–<216 mo. The 1–<12 mo group began at age 29 days because neonatal records had been excluded.2.3Microbiological and diagnosis-coded case definitionIn routine institutional practice, M. pneumoniae-associated illness was diagnosed by treating clinicians based on compatible clinical manifestations, radiologic findings when available, and supportive laboratory evidence, including serological evidence or pathogen detection in respiratory specimens. Laboratory evidence included serology and, when available, molecular detection by polymerase chain reaction (PCR), nucleic acid amplification testing (NAAT), targeted next-generation sequencing (tNGS), or metagenomic next-generation sequencing (mNGS). This approach was consistent with pediatric guideline recommendations and current laboratory guidance supporting the combined use of clinical features and microbiological evidence, while recognizing that NAAT-based methods provide more specific diagnostic support than single-serology evidence (2, 16). In the full discharge-abstract cohort, however, records were identified from finalized diagnosis-coded discharge records rather than full laboratory adjudication. Therefore, the analytic cohort was defined as diagnosis-coded M. pneumoniae-associated hospitalization records, not laboratory-adjudicated incident M. pneumoniae infections.2.4Pathogen-related coded co-diagnosesPathogen-related coded co-diagnoses were derived from specific pathogen-related discharge diagnosis labels. For each pathogen group, a hospitalization record was counted once if one or more corresponding pathogen-specific diagnosis labels were present; repeated labels within the same hospitalization record were not counted more than once. Non-specific infection labels such as bacterial infection, viral infection, infectious fever, respiratory tract infection, and pulmonary infection were not included in the any-pathogen summary variable. Pertussis-like syndrome and parapertussis were not counted as pertussis. Original source-language diagnosis strings are provided for reproducibility.2.5Diagnosis-coded phenotype groups and PICU-associated hospitalizationSelected pulmonary complication, extrapulmonary, severe-care, and hematologic phenotype groups were derived from discharge diagnosis labels according to predefined grouping rules (Supplementary Table S1). Each hospitalization record was counted once for a phenotype group if one or more corresponding discharge diagnosis labels were present; repeated labels within the same hospitalization record were not counted more than once. These grouped variables were defined and interpreted as diagnosis-coded phenotype groups rather than clinically adjudicated organ involvement directly attributable to M. pneumoniae. For example, cardiac abnormality/coded myocardial involvement included discharge labels such as myocardial injury, myocarditis, abnormal myocardial enzyme profile, or electrocardiographic abnormality, whereas neurologic/central nervous system (CNS)-related diagnoses included neurologic or seizure-related discharge labels. The original source-language diagnosis strings and grouping rules are provided in Supplementary Table S1 for reproducibility.PICU-associated hospitalization was defined as any hospitalization record indicating that the child received pediatric intensive care at any time during the hospital stay, based on the structured PICU field and/or department information. This definition included both direct PICU care at hospital presentation and transfer to PICU after admission to another ward. Therefore, the outcome reflects hospitalization involving PICU care rather than direct admission to the PICU at hospital presentation only.2.6Stratified chart-validation subsetTo evaluate the plausibility and supporting documentation of key discharge-coded variables, we conducted a stratified systematic chart-validation substudy of 762 records. Records were stratified by admission year and PICU-associated status; within each stratum, eligible records were ordered by admission date and selected at approximately regular intervals to improve temporal coverage. The validation subset included 247 PICU-associated records and 515 non-PICU records, intentionally enriching PICU-associated records to better assess coding-derived variables related to intensive-care-associated hospitalization. The validation extraction summarized microbiological evidence for M. pneumoniae, chart-level support for selected coded phenotype and comorbidity variables, documentation of other respiratory pathogen testing, and PICU-associated care reasons among PICU-associated validation records. Because PICU-associated records were intentionally enriched, chart-validation findings were interpreted as validation summaries rather than unweighted full-cohort prevalence estimates.2.7Statistical analysisCategorical variables were summarized as counts and percentages, and continuous variables were summarized as medians with interquartile ranges (IQRs). Age-group comparisons were performed using chi-square tests for categorical variables and Kruskal–Wallis tests for continuous variables. Because of the large sample size and multiple descriptive comparisons, p values were interpreted as exploratory, and interpretation emphasized absolute age-stratified differences rather than statistical significance alone. Monthly hospitalization counts, monthly PICU-associated records, and monthly PICU-associated rates were calculated descriptively.Logistic regression models were used to estimate adjusted odds ratios (aORs) and 95% confidence intervals (CIs) for PICU-associated hospitalization. The parsimonious model included age group, sex, and selected common pathogen-related coded co-diagnoses, including rhinovirus, Haemophilus influenzae, adenovirus, respiratory syncytial virus, and influenza virus. The extended exploratory model additionally adjusted for major chronic/congenital comorbidity, admission year, and season as categorical covariates. Season was assigned according to admission month: spring (March–May), summer (June–August), autumn (September–November), and winter (December–February). The reference categories in the extended model were 72–<144 mo for age group, 2024 for admission year, and autumn for season. Full model estimates and model summaries were reported with the model results. The models were intended to explore associations based on available coded variables rather than identify causal risk factors or construct a definitive clinical prediction model.All statistical tests were two-sided. Analyses were performed in Python version 3.11.2 using pandas, NumPy, SciPy, and statsmodels; figures were generated using Matplotlib. 2.1Study design and data sourceThis retrospective discharge-abstract study used a de-identified structured inpatient discharge dataset from Maternal and Child Health Hospital of Hubei Province. Overall, 16,848 records (51.0%) were from male patients, 872 (2.6%) were PICU-associated, and 4,100 (12.4%) had a hospital stay longer than 7 days. The median age at admission was 52.7 months (IQR, 26.5–84.8), and the median length of stay was 5 days (IQR, 4–6). full_text_sections.discussion: 4DiscussionThis single-center discharge-abstract study identified three major findings. First, diagnosis-coded pediatric M. pneumoniae-associated hospitalization records increased markedly from June 2023 onward, with the highest monthly total observed in November 2023, and the highest monthly PICU-associated burden preceded the peak in total monthly records. Second, age structured the distribution of coded phenotypes: younger children had higher proportions of severe-care and systemic labels, whereas school-aged children had higher proportions of structural pulmonary complication labels. Third, selected pathogen-related coded co-diagnoses and major chronic/congenital comorbidity were associated with PICU-associated hospitalization in an exploratory model.This study adds a hospital-service perspective based on routinely collected discharge abstracts to the literature on pediatric M. pneumoniae re-emergence. Clinically adjudicated cohorts are essential for defining laboratory-confirmed infection, imaging severity, treatment, and individual outcomes. In contrast, our study used a large single-center discharge-abstract dataset to describe monthly diagnosis-coded hospitalization records, age-stratified coding-derived phenotype patterns, pathogen-related coded co-diagnoses, and PICU-associated care. Thus, the principal contribution is not to estimate population incidence, prove acute infection in every record, or attribute organ involvement causally to M. pneumoniae, but to show how diagnosis-coded hospitalizations and severe-care demand were distributed over time and across age groups within a consistent tertiary pediatric service system during the post-pandemic period.The temporal pattern is consistent with international reports of delayed post-pandemic re-emergence of M. pneumoniae, including recent hospital-based pediatric data and surveillance reports (5–8, 17). A recent Italian pediatric tertiary-center study of laboratory-confirmed M. pneumoniae infection from 2017 to 2024 reported a marked post-pandemic increase in MP-related hospitalizations, whereas respiratory support requirements, PICU-related outcomes, and length of stay remained broadly comparable with the pre-pandemic period (7). That clinically adjudicated cohort provides an important clinical reference for interpreting post-pandemic hospital burden, but it differs from the present study in data structure and inference: the Italian study evaluated microbiologically confirmed infection episodes with clinical, laboratory, and radiologic information, whereas our study describes diagnosis-coded hospitalization records and hospital-service burden in a large discharge-abstract dataset. Therefore, our findings complement rather than replicate clinically adjudicated MP cohorts. They should be interpreted as hospital-based diagnosis-coded patterns rather than population incidence or laboratory-confirmed infection incidence. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) also notes that M. pneumoniae infection is not nationally notifiable and that surveillance relies on syndromic, laboratory, outbreak, and special-study data sources (17), further supporting a cautious interpretation of our hospital-based temporal pattern.The age-stratified phenotype pattern should be interpreted as a diagnosis-coded pattern rather than a directly adjudicated biological phenotype. The grouped variables were derived from discharge diagnosis labels and may reflect clinical disease, testing intensity, age-related documentation, clinical coding terms, and referral pathways. This concern is particularly relevant for cardiac abnormality/coded myocardial involvement, neurologic/CNS-related diagnoses, and coded sepsis/septicemia, because these categories included broad discharge-diagnosis labels rather than standardized adjudication of organ involvement. Nevertheless, the observed age-structured distribution remains clinically informative when interpreted within these boundaries. Younger children may have lower respiratory reserve and different thresholds for systemic diagnostic labeling or escalation of care, whereas school-aged children with M. pneumoniae-associated pneumonia may more often show structural pulmonary complication labels such as atelectasis and consolidation. Prior pediatric studies have described severe or refractory M. pneumoniae pneumonia, immune activation, mucus plug formation, macrolide-resistant infection, and cardiac or other extrapulmonary manifestations, supporting the biological plausibility of age-related heterogeneity while also emphasizing the need for standardized clinical, imaging, biomarker, and microbiological definitions in future studies (18–22). In line with reporting principles for studies using routinely collected health data, we therefore emphasized transparent coding rules, source-language diagnosis strings, and cautious interpretation of coding-derived variables (13–15).The pathogen-related co-diagnosis findings require careful distinction between coded co-diagnosis, laboratory co-detection, and true causative coinfection. In the full cohort, we analyzed discharge diagnosis labels rather than systematic laboratory co-detection across all children. In the chart-validation subset, microbiological evidence was summarized at the record level; however, even molecular detection may reflect asymptomatic carriage, prolonged detection, timing of sampling, or detection of a pathogen that was not the primary driver of severity (7, 23). This distinction is particularly important for RSV and influenza virus, because both pathogens can independently cause severe pediatric respiratory disease (9, 10). Recent pediatric studies have shown that respiratory virus or adenovirus co-detection in M. pneumoniae pneumonia may be clinically relevant, but co-detection alone does not establish etiologic causality, infection timing, pathogen burden, or directionality of severity (12, 24–27). Accordingly, the associations between pathogen-related coded co-diagnoses and PICU-associated hospitalization in our dataset should be interpreted as discharge-coded risk signals rather than evidence of causal coinfection.The multivariable findings are best interpreted as exploratory associations based on available coded variables rather than independent causal predictors or a definitive clinical prognostic model. Although the extended model adjusted for age, sex, selected pathogen-related coded co-diagnoses, major chronic/congenital comorbidity, admission year, and season, the full cohort did not contain standardized radiologic severity scores, inflammatory biomarkers, oxygen requirement before PICU transfer, treatment intensity, macrolide-resistance results, or pathogen load. These factors have been evaluated in clinically adjudicated pediatric M. pneumoniae studies and may influence severity, structural pulmonary complications, extrapulmonary involvement, or treatment response (18–22). Therefore, the model should not be used to infer that RSV, influenza virus, or comorbidity causally determined PICU-associated hospitalization. Rather, it should be viewed as a discharge-coded risk-stratification analysis showing which routinely available demographic, comorbidity, calendar-time, and pathogen-coded variables were associated with PICU-associated care in this hospital-based dataset.Several limitations should be considered. First, this was a single-center study conducted in a tertiary maternal and child health hospital and provincial children’s infectious disease center, and the findings may not be generalizable to community hospitals or population-level surveillance settings. Second, the primary dataset was based on structured discharge abstracts; therefore, diagnosis-coded phenotype groups may be influenced by clinical documentation, testing intensity, coding conventions, and referral pathways.
