full_text_sections.conclusion: 5ConclusionIn this large single-center discharge-abstract cohort, diagnosis-coded pediatric M. pneumoniae-associated hospitalization records rose above the 2020–2022 monthly range from June 2023 and peaked in November 2023, with age-structured diagnosis-coded phenotype patterns and measurable PICU-associated burden. The findings may inform hospital-based monitoring systems that consider age structure, coding-derived phenotype patterns, pathogen-related coded co-diagnoses, and intensive-care resource use. They should be interpreted as diagnosis-coded hospital-service patterns rather than laboratory-adjudicated incident infections or population incidence.
full_text_sections.other: 1IntroductionMycoplasma pneumoniae is an important cause of respiratory tract infection and community-acquired pneumonia in children. Although many infections are self-limited, hospitalized pediatric M. pneumoniae pneumonia can be associated with severe or refractory disease, structural pulmonary complications, and extrapulmonary manifestations involving the skin, nervous system, cardiovascular system, gastrointestinal tract, and hematologic system (1–4). Recent evidence-based pediatric guidance in China emphasizes the use of compatible clinical features, imaging, and microbiological evidence for diagnosis, while also recognizing the role of severe and refractory phenotypes in clinical management (2).During the COVID-19 pandemic, non-pharmaceutical interventions markedly altered circulation of respiratory pathogens. After restrictions were relaxed, M. pneumoniae re-emerged in several regions, with delayed but substantial post-pandemic activity reported since late 2023 (5–8). However, a single-center discharge-abstract study cannot estimate community incidence or regional prevalence. Its value lies instead in describing hospital-service burden, coding-derived phenotype structure, and severe-care demand within a consistent institutional dataset.The interpretation of pathogen co-diagnoses is also complex. Respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) and influenza virus are major pediatric respiratory pathogens in their own right (9, 10). Respiratory pathogen co-detection in children with pneumonia may reflect overlapping infections, prolonged shedding, colonization, detection intensity, or coding practice rather than true pathogenic coinfection (11, 12). Therefore, in this study we used the term pathogen-related coded co-diagnosis for the full discharge-abstract cohort and reserved laboratory-supported co-detection for the chart-validation subset.Using de-identified structured discharge abstracts from a tertiary maternal and child health hospital and provincial children’s infectious disease prevention and control center in Hubei, China, this study aimed to characterize monthly hospital-based burden, age-stratified diagnosis-coded phenotypes, pathogen-related coded co-diagnoses, and exploratory variables associated with PICU-associated hospitalization among diagnosis-coded pediatric M. pneumoniae-associated hospitalization records. 2.2Study population and data cleaningThe initial screening dataset contained 34,562 diagnosis-coded M. pneumoniae-associated hospitalization records. Records from children aged <29 days (n = 55), records from patients aged ≥18 years (n = 1,436), and repeated hospitalization records identified through manual verification (n = 24) were excluded. The final analytic dataset included 33,047 eligible pediatric hospitalization records aged ≥29 days and <18 years (Supplementary Figure S1). The unit of analysis was the hospitalization record. Age was calculated at admission and expressed in month-based clinical categories: 1–<12 mo, 12–<36 mo, 36–<72 mo, 72–<144 mo, and 144–<216 mo. The 1–<12 mo group began at age 29 days because neonatal records had been excluded. 2.3Microbiological and diagnosis-coded case definitionIn routine institutional practice, M. pneumoniae-associated illness was diagnosed by treating clinicians based on compatible clinical manifestations, radiologic findings when available, and supportive laboratory evidence, including serological evidence or pathogen detection in respiratory specimens. Laboratory evidence included serology and, when available, molecular detection by polymerase chain reaction (PCR), nucleic acid amplification testing (NAAT), targeted next-generation sequencing (tNGS), or metagenomic next-generation sequencing (mNGS). This approach was consistent with pediatric guideline recommendations and current laboratory guidance supporting the combined use of clinical features and microbiological evidence, while recognizing that NAAT-based methods provide more specific diagnostic support than single-serology evidence (2, 16). In the full discharge-abstract cohort, however, records were identified from finalized diagnosis-coded discharge records rather than full laboratory adjudication. Therefore, the analytic cohort was defined as diagnosis-coded M. pneumoniae-associated hospitalization records, not laboratory-adjudicated incident M. pneumoniae infections. 2.4Pathogen-related coded co-diagnosesPathogen-related coded co-diagnoses were derived from specific pathogen-related discharge diagnosis labels. For each pathogen group, a hospitalization record was counted once if one or more corresponding pathogen-specific diagnosis labels were present; repeated labels within the same hospitalization record were not counted more than once. Non-specific infection labels such as bacterial infection, viral infection, infectious fever, respiratory tract infection, and pulmonary infection were not included in the any-pathogen summary variable. Pertussis-like syndrome and parapertussis were not counted as pertussis. Original source-language diagnosis strings are provided for reproducibility. 2.5Diagnosis-coded phenotype groups and PICU-associated hospitalizationSelected pulmonary complication, extrapulmonary, severe-care, and hematologic phenotype groups were derived from discharge diagnosis labels according to predefined grouping rules (Supplementary Table S1). Each hospitalization record was counted once for a phenotype group if one or more corresponding discharge diagnosis labels were present; repeated labels within the same hospitalization record were not counted more than once. These grouped variables were defined and interpreted as diagnosis-coded phenotype groups rather than clinically adjudicated organ involvement directly attributable to M. pneumoniae. For example, cardiac abnormality/coded myocardial involvement included discharge labels such as myocardial injury, myocarditis, abnormal myocardial enzyme profile, or electrocardiographic abnormality, whereas neurologic/central nervous system (CNS)-related diagnoses included neurologic or seizure-related discharge labels. The original source-language diagnosis strings and grouping rules are provided in Supplementary Table S1 for reproducibility.PICU-associated hospitalization was defined as any hospitalization record indicating that the child received pediatric intensive care at any time during the hospital stay, based on the structured PICU field and/or department information. This definition included both direct PICU care at hospital presentation and transfer to PICU after admission to another ward. Therefore, the outcome reflects hospitalization involving PICU care rather than direct admission to the PICU at hospital presentation only. 2.6Stratified chart-validation subsetTo evaluate the plausibility and supporting documentation of key discharge-coded variables, we conducted a stratified systematic chart-validation substudy of 762 records. Records were stratified by admission year and PICU-associated status; within each stratum, eligible records were ordered by admission date and selected at approximately regular intervals to improve temporal coverage. The validation subset included 247 PICU-associated records and 515 non-PICU records, intentionally enriching PICU-associated records to better assess coding-derived variables related to intensive-care-associated hospitalization. The validation extraction summarized microbiological evidence for M. pneumoniae, chart-level support for selected coded phenotype and comorbidity variables, documentation of other respiratory pathogen testing, and PICU-associated care reasons among PICU-associated validation records. Because PICU-associated records were intentionally enriched, chart-validation findings were interpreted as validation summaries rather than unweighted full-cohort prevalence estimates. 2.7Statistical analysisCategorical variables were summarized as counts and percentages, and continuous variables were summarized as me…

papers.title_original: Age-related heterogeneity in diagnosis-coded pediatric Mycoplasma pneumoniae-associated hospitalizations and PICU-associated care: a single-center retrospective study

analysis.research_question_and_background: The study aimed to investigate age-related differences in diagnosis-coded hospitalizations associated with Mycoplasma pneumoniae and the burden of PICU-associated care in pediatric patients. This is important due to the potential variability in clinical manifestations and outcomes across different age groups.
analysis.study_design_and_population: A single-center retrospective study was conducted using diagnosis-coded discharge records from a tertiary maternal and child health hospital in Hubei, China. The analytic dataset included 33,047 pediatric hospitalization records aged ≥29 days and <18 years, with 872 records associated with PICU care.
analysis.methods: The study used a de-identified structured inpatient discharge dataset and conducted a stratified systematic chart-validation substudy of 762 records to evaluate key discharge-coded variables. Logistic regression models were employed to estimate adjusted odds ratios (aORs) and 95% confidence intervals (CIs) for PICU-associated hospitalization, with the parsimonious model including age group, sex, and selected pathogen-related coded co-diagnoses.
analysis.main_results: In 2023, monthly records of M. pneumoniae-associated hospitalizations increased from 99 in January and 139 in February to 2,282 in November. Respiratory failure/hypoxemia was recorded in 6.6% of the 1–<12 mo group versus 1.3% of the 72–<144 mo group; coded sepsis/septicemia in 11.2% versus 5.9%; and cardiac abnormality/coded myocardial involvement in 25.0% versus 15.6%.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The findings highlight age-related heterogeneity in diagnosis-coded phenotypes and PICU-associated burden, suggesting that younger children have a higher likelihood of severe clinical manifestations compared to older age groups. This provides novel insights into the clinical patterns of M. pneumoniae-associated hospitalizations across different pediatric age strata.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: These results can inform targeted surveillance and clinical management strategies for pediatric M. pneumoniae infections, particularly in younger age groups who show a higher risk of PICU-associated care. They may also guide resource allocation and early intervention protocols in hospital settings.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study is based on diagnosis-coded records, which may lack specificity compared to laboratory-confirmed cases. The evidence is moderate, as it reflects hospital-based patterns rather than population incidence, and the findings are limited to a single-center retrospective analysis.

analysis.summary_en: This study investigated age-related differences in diagnosis-coded hospitalizations associated with Mycoplasma pneumoniae and the burden of PICU-associated care in pediatric patients at a tertiary maternal and child health hospital in Hubei, China. A retrospective design was used, with a stratified chart-validation subset of 762 records to evaluate key variables. The analytic dataset included 33,047 eligible pediatric hospitalizations, of which 872 were PICU-associated. Results showed a significant increase in monthly hospitalization records in 2023, peaking in November. Age-stratified analysis revealed higher rates of severe clinical manifestations, such as respiratory failure/hypoxemia, coded sepsis/septicemia, and cardiac abnormality, in younger children compared to older age groups. The findings highlight the need for age-specific clinical management and surveillance strategies for M. pneumoniae infections. However, the study is limited to diagnosis-coded data, which may lack precision, and is based on a single-center retrospective design, which may affect generalizability. The evidence is moderate in strength due to these limitations.

elements_zh.methods: 本研究使用了匿名化的结构化住院出院数据集,并对762份记录进行了分层系统图表验证子研究,以评估关键的出院编码变量。采用逻辑回归模型估计与PICU相关住院的调整比值比(aORs)和95%置信区间(CIs),其中简明模型包括年龄组、性别和选定的病原体相关编码合并诊断。
elements_zh.main_results: 2023年,肺炎支原体相关住院的月记录从1月的99例和2月的139例增加到11月的2,282例。1–<12月龄组记录了6.6%的呼吸衰竭/低氧血症,而72–<144月龄组为1.3%;记录了11.2%的脓毒症/败血症,而72–<144月龄组为5.9%;记录了25.0%的心脏异常/编码心肌受累,而72–<144月龄组为15.6%。
elements_zh.interpretation_and_novelty: 研究结果突出了诊断编码表型和与PICU相关负担在不同年龄组中的异质性,表明年幼儿童比年长年龄组更有可能出现严重的临床表现。这为不同儿科年龄分层中肺炎支原体相关住院的临床模式提供了新的见解。
elements_zh.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: 这些结果可以为针对儿科肺炎支原体感染的监测和临床管理策略提供信息,特别是对那些表现出更高PICU相关护理风险的年轻年龄组。它们也可能指导医院环境中的资源分配和早期干预协议。
elements_zh.limitations_and_evidence_strength: 本研究基于诊断编码记录,可能缺乏与实验室确认病例相比的特异性。证据强度中等,因为其反映了医院内的模式,而非人群发病率,且研究结果仅限于单中心回顾性分析。

analysis_en.research_question_and_background: The study aimed to investigate age-related differences in diagnosis-coded hospitalizations associated with Mycoplasma pneumoniae and the burden of PICU-associated care in pediatric patients. This is important due to the potential variability in clinical manifestations and outcomes across different age groups.
analysis_en.study_design_and_population: A single-center retrospective study was conducted using diagnosis-coded discharge records from a tertiary maternal and child health hospital in Hubei, China. The analytic dataset included 33,047 pediatric hospitalization records aged ≥29 days and <18 years, with 872 records associated with PICU care.
analysis_en.methods: The study used a de-identified structured inpatient discharge dataset and conducted a stratified systematic chart-validation substudy of 762 records to evaluate key discharge-coded variables. Logistic regression models were employed to estimate adjusted odds ratios (aORs) and 95% confidence intervals (CIs) for PICU-associated hospitalization, with the parsimonious model including age group, sex, and selected pathogen-related coded co-diagnoses.
analysis_en.main_results: In 2023, monthly records of M. pneumoniae-associated hospitalizations increased from 99 in January and 139 in February to 2,282 in November. Respiratory failure/hypoxemia was recorded in 6.6% of the 1–<12 mo group versus 1.3% of the 72–<144 mo group; coded sepsis/septicemia in 11.2% versus 5.9%; and cardiac abnormality/coded myocardial involvement in 25.0% versus 15.6%.
analysis_en.interpretation_and_novelty: The findings highlight age-related heterogeneity in diagnosis-coded phenotypes and PICU-associated burden, suggesting that younger children have a higher likelihood of severe clinical manifestations compared to older age groups. This provides novel insights into the clinical patterns of M. pneumoniae-associated hospitalizations across different pediatric age strata.
analysis_en.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: These results can inform targeted surveillance and clinical management strategies for pediatric M. pneumoniae infections, particularly in younger age groups who show a higher risk of PICU-associated care. They may also guide resource allocation and early intervention protocols in hospital settings.
analysis_en.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study is based on diagnosis-coded records, which may lack specificity compared to laboratory-confirmed cases. The evidence is moderate, as it reflects hospital-based patterns rather than population incidence, and the findings are limited to a single-center retrospective analysis.

papers.full_text: ObjectiveDistinguishing lower respiratory tract infections (LRTIs) from noninfectious pulmonary infiltrates (NPIs) in patients with lymphoma is challenging. We assessed the diagnostic value of bronchoalveolar lavage fluid (BALF) cytokine and lymphocyte profiles (CPs and LPs).MethodsThis retrospective study included 147 participants: 55 lymphoma patients with LRTIs, 52 with NPIs, and 40 non-lymphoma patients with LRTIs. Fourteen BALF cytokines and ten BALF and peripheral blood lymphocyte measures were assessed by multiparameter flow cytometry. LASSO-selected logistic regression models were developed using five-fold cross-validation. full_text_sections.abstract: ObjectiveDistinguishing lower respiratory tract infections (LRTIs) from noninfectious pulmonary infiltrates (NPIs) in patients with lymphoma is challenging. We assessed the diagnostic value of bronchoalveolar lavage fluid (BALF) cytokine and lymphocyte profiles (CPs and LPs).MethodsThis retrospective study included 147 participants: 55 lymphoma patients with LRTIs, 52 with NPIs, and 40 non-lymphoma patients with LRTIs. Fourteen BALF cytokines and ten BALF and peripheral blood lymphocyte measures were assessed by multiparameter flow cytometry. LASSO-selected logistic regression models were developed using five-fold cross-validation. BALF models incorporated CPs and LPs, whereas Base models used routine inflammatory markers, with or without sputum production. Models were compared using DeLong tests, NRI, IDI, and 1,000-resample bootstrap optimism correction.ResultsLASSO retained BALF IL-8 and CD3 + CD4 + for BALF models and CRP and SAA for Base models. Test-set AUCs were 0.845 and 0.853 for BALF-A and BALF-B, vs. 0.973 and 0.969 for Base-A and Base-B, respectively. Base models significantly outperformed corresponding BALF models. Optimism-corrected AUCs were 0.872 for both BALF models and 0.980 and 0.977 for Base-A and Base-B. Adding sputum production improved BALF-model reclassification without significantly increasing AUC and provided no benefit to Base models. Eight immune parameters differed by lymphoma status among patients with LRTIs, with additional infection-type-specific patterns.ConclusionsBALF IL-8/CD4-based models distinguished LRTIs from NPIs in patients with lymphoma, although CRP/SAA-based models performed better. BALF immune profiling may complement conventional biomarkers and reveal immune signatures associated with lymphoma status and infection type.

full_text_sections.results: ResultsDifferential baseline characteristics across the three cohortsA total of 147 participants were enrolled between January 1, 2022, and April 30, 2023, at the Aerospace Center Hospital. These patients comprised 55 lymphoma patients with confirmed LRTIs, 52 lymphoma patients who underwent bronchoscopy for pulmonary infiltrates and were adjudicated as having NPIs after comprehensive evaluation, including clinical presentation, chest imaging, and BALF microbiological testing, and 40 non-lymphoma patients with confirmed LRTIs. Table 1 illustrated the baseline of the participants, comparing two groups: Lym + LRTIs vs. Lym + NPIs cohorts, and Lym + LRTIs vs. non-Lym + LRTIs cohorts. The Lym + LRTIs cohort had a significantly higher incidence of sputum production (SP) compared to the Lym + NPIs cohort (P < 0.001). Additionally, these two cohorts differed significantly in lymphoma types (P < 0.01). Regarding laboratory findings, the Lym + LRTIs cohort had higher levels of white blood cell count, neutrophil percentage, CRP, PCT, SAA, and 1,3-beta-D-glucan compared to the Lym + NPIs cohort (P < 0.05). While the level of lymphocyte percentage was lower than that in Lym + NPIs cohort (P < 0.001). When comparing the Lym + LRTIs cohort to the non-Lym + LRTIs cohort, the former showed lower white blood cell counts and higher monocyte percentages (P < 0.001).Table 1Baseline characteristics of 147 full_text_sections.discussion: DiscussionIn this retrospective study of 147 patients, we developed and internally validated LR models based on BALF CPs and LPs to distinguish LRTIs from NPIs in patients with lymphoma. Several findings warrant emphasis. First, a parsimonious BALF model comprising IL-8, CD3 + CD4+ T cells, and sputum production achieved good discrimination, with a test-set AUC of 0.853 and an optimism-corrected AUC of 0.872 after 1,000-bootstrap validation. Second, although adding sputum production to the BALF model did not significantly improve the AUC (P = 0.791), it significantly improved risk reclassification (NRI = 0.666, 95% CI: 0.316∼0.976). Third, models based on routine inflammatory markers (CRP and SAA) significantly outperformed the BALF models (optimism-corrected AUCs of 0.977∼0.980; DeLong P < 0.01) and were considerably more robust to overfitting.The selection of IL-8 is biologically plausible. Previous research in patients with non-Hodgkin lymphoma showed that IL-8 and other cytokines were elevated during respiratory bacterial infections (2). Single-cell analyses have also linked increased pulmonary CXCL8 expression to neutrophil accumulation and lung injury in severe viral and bacterial pneumonia (11, 14). These findings support BALF IL-8 as a marker of local infectious inflammation. In the lower respiratory tract, alveolar macrophages are major producers of IL-8, although type II pneumocytes, fibroblasts, and endothelial cells also contribute (15). IL-8 promotes adhesion-molecule expression and recruits neutrophils—key defenders against bacterial and fungal pathogens—into infected lung tissue (16). Binding to CXCR1 and CXCR2 further activates neutrophil metabolic and morphological responses (17). These mechanisms may explain elevated BALF IL-8 levels in patients with LRTIs and underscore its role in pulmonary host defense. Conversely, higher BALF CD3 + CD4 + proportions were associated with lower odds of LRTIs (odds ratio 0.968∼0.972 per percentage point), suggesting that preserved local T-cell immunity protects against infection. This notion is consistent with the central role of CD4+ T cells in pulmonary host defense against bacterial, viral, and fungal pathogens (18) and, conversely, with the increased susceptibility to LRTIs imposed by lymphoma and antineoplastic treatment. One additional point requires separate clarification. Lymphoma subtype distributions differed between the Lym + LRTIs and Lym + NPIs cohorts (Table 1, P = 0.004). In a sensitivity analysis restricted to B-NHL, IL-8 remained significantly different between groups (P < 0.001), whereas BALF CD3 + CD4 + did not (P = 0.180). Thus, although the IL-8 signal was robust, the overall IL-8/CD4/sputum production model as a whole should be viewed as a classifier derived from a subtype-imbalanced cohort.An important and perhaps unexpected finding was that the Base models significantly outperformed the BALF models. Several explanations should be considered. First, CRP and SAA are potent acute-phase reactants reflecting large, systemic responses, whereas BALF cytokines are local signals susceptible to lavage dilution, variable fluid recovery, and the focal distribution of infiltrates. Second, the BALF models showed greater overfitting (corrected calibration slopes 0.50∼0.53 vs. 0.71∼0.77 for the Base models); with only 107 patients, parsimonious two-variable models are inherently more stable. We therefore emphasize that the BALF model is not intended to replace routine inflammatory markers, which remain accurate, inexpensive, and universally available (19). Its potential value may instead lie in patients with atypical presentations or discordant clinical, radiological, microbiological, and systemic inflammatory findings (20).Adding sputum production to the BALF model significantly improved the NRI but did not significantly increase the AUC, while the IDI improvement was borderline. This suggests that sputum production may alter the ranking of individual predictions without materially improving overall discrimination. NRI findings should be interpreted cautiously because they are sensitive to model calibration and the definition of clinically meaningful risk categories (21). Conversely, sputum production conferred no benefit to the Base model, possibly because its diagnostic information was already captured by CRP and SAA. Future studies should evaluate incremental predictors using prespecified probability thresholds and decision-curve analysis.The secondary analysis revealed differences in BALF IL-6, IL-8, IFN-γ, and several T-, B-, and NK-cell subsets between patients with and without lymphoma who had LRTIs, as well as infection type-specific variations. Collectively, these findings suggest that lymphoma and its treatment may reshape the pulmonary immune milieu during infection (14). Nevertheless, the results should be considered exploratory because the viral-only and bacterial-only subgroups were small and multiple immune parameters were tested without adjustment for multiple comparisons. SARS-CoV-2 was the most frequently detected pathogen, accounting for 23.2% of LRTIs, consistent with enrollment overlapping the Omicron era in China. This temporal context should be considered when generalizing our findings to other periods and settings.Several limitations should be acknowledged. This retrospective, single-center study included a modest number of patients who underwent bronchoscopy, potentially introducing selection bias. Internal validation cannot replace independent prospective validation. Moreover, heterogeneity in lymphoma subtype and treatment may have confounded the observed BALF associations, while variations in BALF dilution, sampling site, and timing relative to antimicrobial therapy may have influenced biomarker concentrations.
full_text_sections.conclusion: ConclusionA BALF cytokine-lymphocyte profile-based model incorporating IL-8, CD3 + CD4+, and sputum production accurately distinguished LRTIs from NPIs in patients with lymphoma, although the model based on routine inflammatory markers (CRP and SAA) performed significantly better. BALF immune profiling may therefore complement conventional biomarkers and reveal distinct local immune signatures associated with lymphoma status and infection type. External validation is required before clinical implementation.
full_text_sections.other: IntroductionLymphoma, a malignancy arising from lymphocytes, is frequently complicated by infection. Lower respiratory tract infections (LRTIs) are particularly common in patients with lymphoma, largely because of disease- and treatment-related immunosuppression (1). Prompt recognition and management are essential, as severe infections may cause additional complications and increase mortality risk (2). However, diagnosing LRTIs in patients with lymphoma remains challenging for two main reasons (3). First, high-resolution computed tomography findings of chemotherapy-induced lung injury often overlap with those of LRTIs, and mixed infections further complicate etiological diagnosis. Second, conventional cultures of respiratory specimens detect a limited pathogen range, with slow turnaround and low sensitivity. Moreover, immunosuppression may cause infected lymphoma patients to present with mild or absent fever and normal serum inflammatory markers, further obscuring diagnosis (4). Lymphoma and its treatment may also alter systemic and pulmonary immune-cell profiles; characterizing these alterations could improve our understanding of immune dysregulation in patients with lymphoma and LRTIs.Bronchoalveolar lavage fluid (BALF), sampled directly from the affected pulmonary segment, reflects local inflammatory and immune responses within the lung. Compared with sputum, BALF provides a more direct assessment of the pulmonary microenvironment, particularly when clinical and radiological findings are insufficient for a definitive diagnosis. Analysis of its cellular and particulate components, including resident and recruited immune cells, together with soluble constituents such as immunoglobulins, enzymes, and antimicrobial peptides and proteins, provides deeper insight into the local immune milieu and may help distinguish LRTIs from noninfectious pulmonary infiltrates (NPIs) (5, 6).In recent years, cytokine profiles (CPs) and lymphocyte profiles (LPs) have emerged as potential biomarkers of infection (7). In lymphoma patients, conventional inflammatory markers remain valuable because they are widely available, routinely measured, and often distinguish infectious from noninfectious conditions. However, they mainly reflect systemic inflammatory burden and offer limited insight into immune mechanisms. CPs and LPs may provide complementary diagnostic information, especially in atypical presentations. More importantly, many cytokines and T-cell subsets are directly involved in LRTIs pathogenesis (8), so they may better reflect disease pathophysiology and represent potential therapeutic targets (9). A distinct BALF signature comprising elevated IL-8 and IL-13 and increased neutrophils distinguished nontuberculous mycobacterial pulmonary disease from noninfectious granulomatous lung disorders (10). In non-Hodgkin lymphoma, IL-6 and IL-8 outperformed fever, procalcitonin (PCT), and CRP for early detection of respiratory bacterial infection, particularly in minimally symptomatic patients (2). Moreover, single-cell transcriptomics identified a CXCL8 (IL-8)-neutrophil recruitment axis as a key determinant of pneumonia severity (11).Previous studies have primarily focused on analyzing CPs and LPs in peripheral blood (PB) for LRTIs diagnosis. However, lower respiratory tract specimens obtained directly from the infection site offer distinct advantages in differentiating LRTIs, making the analysis of CPs and LPs in BALF essential. Our analyses addressed two distinct clinical and biological questions. The primary analysis compared lymphoma patients with LRTIs (Lym + LRTIs) versus those with noninfectious pulmonary infiltrates (Lym + NPIs), thereby addressing a clinically relevant differential diagnosis in lymphoma patients presenting with pulmonary infiltrates, in whom infectious and noninfectious etiologies must be distinguished. In contrast, the secondary analysis focused on patients with confirmed LRTIs and compared pulmonary immune profiles according to lymphoma status. Bronchoalveolar lavage procedure and fluid collectionBALF was collected before antibiotic therapy or 48∼72 h after discontinuing prior antibiotics. In most cases, bronchoalveolar lavage was targeted toward affected lung segments as noted on chest computed tomography and performed with 50 mL of 0.9% sterile normal saline per lavage. Usually, three lavages were performed, with greater than or equal to 30% of the total lavage fluid being retrieved through gentle suction and filtered through sterile gauze to remove mucus strands (12). We conducted etiological examination on the collected BALF, including smear staining (Gram staining, Ziehl-Neelsen staining, and Periodic-acid silver methenamine staining), cultures (for bacteria, fungi, and mycobacteria), respiratory virus PCR (for SARS-CoV-2, Influenza A, Influenza B, Respiratory syncytial virus (RSV), Adenovirus, Human rhinovirus, Cytomegalovirus (CMV), Epstein–Barr virus (EBV), and Mycoplasma pneumoniae (MP)), and metagenomic next-generation sequencing (mNGS). The remaining BALF samples were centrifuged, and the supernatants and precipitates were separated for cytokines and lymphocyte subsets analysis, respectively. The PB samples were collected in EDTA-K2 anticoagulant tubes (≥2 mL) for lymphocyte subset analysis using anticoagulated whole blood. Measurement of cytokine and lymphocyte profilesThe concentrations of CPs in BALF, LPs in BALF, and LPs in PB were analyzed using multiparameter flow cytometry on the DxFLEX (Beckman Coulter Life Sciences, Indianapolis, IN, USA). The human custom 14-cytokine kit, which measures IL-1β, IL-2, IL-4, IL-5, IL-6, IL-8, IL-10, IL-12p70, IL-17A, IL-17F, IL-22, TNF-α, TNF-β, and IFN-γ, was purchased from Quantobio Biotechnology (Beijing, China), and assays were conducted according to the manufacturer's protocol. All BALF samples were analyzed using bead-based multiplex flow cytometry and were diluted 1:3 prior to testing. LPs, including CD3+, CD3 + CD4+, CD3 + CD8+, CD19+, and CD16 + CD56 + in both BALF and PB, were identified using a kit from Quantobio Biotechnology, which contained fluorescently labeled antibodies: CD3-FITC, CD16 + 56-PE, CD45-PerCP-Cy5.5, CD4-PC7, CD19-APC, and CD8-APC-Cy7. All samples, along with the manufacturer's quality control products, were immediately tested to ensure the accuracy of the detection. Data analysis was subsequently performed using Kaluza software (V2.1.1). Based on LASSO analysis and logistic regression model for discriminating Lym + LRTIs and Lym + NPIsBaseline CRP, PCT, and serum amyloid A (SAA) were used to develop the Base logistic regression (LR) models, while 24 CP and LP features were evaluated for the BALF models. All variables were initially eligible for selection using least absolute shrinkage and selection operator (LASSO) within five-fold cross-validation. In each iteration, four folds formed the training set and the remaining fold served as the test set. To avoid information leakage, imputation parameters, feature selection, and model fitting were derived exclusively from the training data before being applied to the held-out fold. The regularization parameter λ was determined using the one-standard-error rule, and features selected in at least 80% of the folds were retained for final modeling. Fold-specific receiver operating characteristic curves and calibration plots were averaged across iterations. Discrimination and calibration were assessed separately in the training and test sets using the area under the curve (AUC) and Brier score, with 95% confidence intervals. Additional performance measures included accuracy, sensitivity, specificity, positive and negative predictive values, F1 score, and Cohen's kappa. Finally, the retained predictors were refitted using the full dataset to derive the Base and BALF models, expressed aslogit(P)=β0+β1X1+⋯+βkXk. papers.title_original: Diagnostic value of bronchoalveolar lavage fluid cytokine and lymphocyte profiles for lower respiratory tract infections in patients with lymphoma

analysis.research_question_and_background: The study aimed to evaluate the diagnostic utility of bronchoalveolar lavage fluid (BALF) cytokine and lymphocyte profiles for lower respiratory tract infections (LRTIs) in patients with lymphoma, addressing the need for improved diagnostic tools in this vulnerable population.
analysis.study_design_and_population: This retrospective study included 147 participants: 55 lymphoma patients with LRTIs, 52 with non-pulmonary infections (NPIs), and 40 non-lymphoma patients with LRTIs. Exclusion criteria included diagnoses of malignant solid tumors, other hematologic diseases, or autoimmune disorders, as well as diseases requiring prolonged use of specific medications.
analysis.methods: BALF cytokines and lymphocyte subsets were analyzed using multiparameter flow cytometry, with samples diluted 1:3 prior to testing. Etiological examination included smear staining, cultures, respiratory virus PCR for SARS-CoV-2, Influenza A, Influenza B, RSV, Adenovirus, Human rhinovirus, CMV, EBV, and MP, and metagenomic next-generation sequencing (mNGS). Logistic regression models were developed using LASSO feature selection and five-fold cross-validation, with missing values imputed using the median from training folds.
analysis.main_results: Four logistic regression models were developed, with test-set AUCs ranging from 0.845 to 0.973. The Base models, which included CRP and SAA, showed superior overall performance compared to the BALF models.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The authors interpreted that the Base models outperformed BALF models in diagnosing LRTIs in lymphoma patients, suggesting that traditional biomarkers may be more effective than BALF cytokine and lymphocyte profiles in this context.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: These findings may inform the development of more accurate diagnostic strategies for LRTIs in immunocompromised patients, potentially improving clinical decision-making and treatment outcomes.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study is limited by its retrospective design and potential for missing data, though the use of five-fold cross-validation and median imputation strengthens the evidence. Confidence in the results is moderate due to these limitations.

analysis.summary_en: This study evaluated the diagnostic value of bronchoalveolar lavage fluid (BALF) cytokine and lymphocyte profiles for lower respiratory tract infections (LRTIs) in patients with lymphoma. A retrospective design included 147 participants, divided into three groups: lymphoma patients with LRTIs (55), lymphoma patients with non-pulmonary infections (NPIs) (52), and non-lymphoma patients with LRTIs (40). Methods involved multiparameter flow cytometry for cytokine and lymphocyte analysis, alongside etiological examination using PCR and metagenomic next-generation sequencing. Four logistic regression models were developed, with the Base models (using CRP and SAA) showing superior performance in distinguishing LRTIs from NPIs. The study highlights the potential of traditional biomarkers over BALF profiles in this population, though limitations such as missing data and retrospective design suggest moderate confidence in the findings.

elements_zh.research_question_and_background: 本研究旨在评估支气管肺泡灌洗液(BALF)中的细胞因子和淋巴细胞谱对淋巴瘤患者下呼吸道感染(LRTIs)的诊断价值,以应对这一易感人群中对改进诊断工具的需求。
elements_zh.study_design_and_population: 这项回顾性研究共纳入147名参与者:55名淋巴瘤合并下呼吸道感染(LRTIs)的患者,52名合并非肺部感染(NPIs)的患者,以及40名非淋巴瘤合并下呼吸道感染的患者。排除标准包括恶性实体肿瘤、其他血液系统疾病或自身免疫性疾病的诊断,以及需要长期使用特定药物的疾病。
elements_zh.methods: 通过多参数流式细胞术分析BALF细胞因子和淋巴细胞亚群,样本在检测前按1:3比例稀释。病原学检查包括涂片染色、培养、针对SARS-CoV-2、流感A型、流感B型、呼吸道合胞病毒、腺病毒、人类鼻病毒、巨细胞病毒、EB病毒和支原体的呼吸道病毒PCR,以及宏基因组下一代测序(mNGS)。使用LASSO特征选择和五折交叉验证开发了逻辑回归模型,缺失值通过训练折的中位数进行填补。
elements_zh.main_results: 开发了四种逻辑回归模型,测试集AUC值范围从0.845到0.973。包含CRP和SAA的基础模型整体表现优于BALF模型。

elements_zh.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: 这些发现可能有助于为免疫功能低下患者的下呼吸道感染(LRTIs)开发更准确的诊断策略,从而潜在改善临床决策和治疗结局。
elements_zh.limitations_and_evidence_strength: 该研究受到其回顾性设计和潜在数据缺失的限制,尽管使用了五折交叉验证和中位数填补方法增强了证据的可信度。由于这些限制,结果的可信度中等。

analysis_en.interpretation_and_novelty: The authors interpreted that the Base models outperformed BALF models in diagnosing LRTIs in lymphoma patients, suggesting that traditional biomarkers may be more effective than BALF cytokine and lymphocyte profiles in this context.
analysis_en.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: These findings may inform the development of more accurate diagnostic strategies for LRTIs in immunocompromised patients, potentially improving clinical decision-making and treatment outcomes.
analysis_en.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study is limited by its retrospective design and potential for missing data, though the use of five-fold cross-validation and median imputation strengthens the evidence. Confidence in the results is moderate due to these limitations.

papers.title_zh: 淋巴瘤患者下呼吸道感染中支气管肺泡灌洗液细胞因子和淋巴细胞谱的诊断价值
papers.source_body_en: We assessed the diagnostic value of bronchoalveolar lavage fluid (BALF) cytokine and lymphocyte profiles (CPs and LPs).MethodsThis retrospective study included 147 participants: 55 lymphoma patients with LRTIs, 52 with NPIs, and 40 non-lymphoma patients with LRTIs. MethodsPatient screening and enrollmentThe inclusion criteria were as follows: (1) age ≥ 18 years; (2) a clinical diagnosis of lymphoma based on the 5th edition of the WHO Classification of Haematolymphoid Tumors; (3) fulfillment of the diagnostic criteria for LRTIs as outlined by the Chinese Thoracic Society (CTS) in 2016 and 2018 (Supplementary Table S1), confirmed by at least two pulmonologists and one microbiologist; (4) provision of informed consent and voluntary participation in the study; and (5) availability of complete data on cytokine levels and lymphocyte subsets. This was a retrospective observational study. Demographics, symptoms, comorbidities, clinical scores, routine laboratory findings, and etiological data were reviewed through electronic medical records. We conducted etiological examination on the collected BALF, including smear staining (Gram staining, Ziehl-Neelsen staining, and Periodic-acid silver methenamine staining), cultures (for bacteria, fungi, and mycobacteria), respiratory virus PCR (for SARS-CoV-2, Influenza A, Influenza B, Respiratory syncytial virus (RSV), Adenovirus, Human rhinovirus, Cytomegalovirus (CMV), Epstein–Barr virus (EBV), and Mycoplasma pneumoniae (MP)), and metagenomic next-generation sequencing (mNGS). ObjectiveDistinguishing lower respiratory tract infections (LRTIs) from noninfectious pulmonary infiltrates (NPIs) in patients with lymphoma is challenging. Fourteen BALF cytokines and ten BALF and peripheral blood lymphocyte measures were assessed by multiparame...
papers.abstract_zh: 我们评估了支气管肺泡灌洗液(BALF)细胞因子和淋巴细胞谱(CPs和LPs)的诊断价值。方法本回顾性研究包括147名参与者:55名淋巴瘤合并下呼吸道感染(LRTIs)的患者,52名非肺部感染(NPIs)的患者,以及40名非淋巴瘤合并LRTIs的患者。患者筛选和纳入标准纳入标准如下:(1)年龄≥18岁;(2)根据世界卫生组织(WHO)第5版血液淋巴肿瘤分类的临床诊断为淋巴瘤;(3)符合中国胸科学会(CTS)2016年和2018年制定的LRTIs诊断标准(补充表S1),由至少两名肺科医生和一名微生物学家确认;(4)签署知情同意书并自愿参与研究;(5)具备完整的细胞因子水平和淋巴细胞亚群数据。这是一项回顾性观察性研究。通过电子病历回顾了人口统计学、症状、合并症、临床评分、常规实验室检查结果和病原学数据。对收集的BALF进行了病原学检查,包括涂片染色(革兰染色、齐-尼尔森染色和过碘酸雪夫染色)、培养(细菌、真菌和分枝杆菌)、呼吸道病毒PCR(SARS-CoV-2、流感A、流感B、呼吸道合胞病毒(RSV)、腺病毒、人类鼻病毒、巨细胞病毒(CMV)、EB病毒(EBV)和肺炎支原体(MP)),以及宏基因组下一代测序(mNGS)。目标在淋巴瘤患者中区分下呼吸道感染(LRTIs)和非感染性肺浸润(NPIs)具有挑战性。通过多参数流式细胞术分析了14种BALF细胞因子和10种BALF及外周血淋巴细胞指标,样本在检测前稀释为1:3。病原学检查包括涂片染色、培养、呼吸道病毒PCR(SARS-CoV-2、流感A、流感B、RSV、腺病毒、人类鼻病毒、CMV、EBV和MP)以及宏基因组下一代测序(mNGS)。使用LASSO特征选择和五折交叉验证开发了逻辑回归模型,并使用训练折的中位数对缺失值进行插补。主要结果开发了四个逻辑回归模型,测试集AUC值范围为0.845至0.973。包含CRP和SAA的基线模型整体表现优于BALF模型。解释与创新性作者认为,基线模型在诊断淋巴瘤患者LRTIs方面优于BALF模型,表明传统生物标志物可能在此背景下比BALF细胞因子和淋巴细胞谱更有效。科学与公共卫生意义这些发现可能有助于为免疫功能低下患者开发更准确的LRTIs诊断策略,从而改善临床决策和治疗结果。局限性与证据强度该研究受到回顾性设计和潜在数据缺失的限制,尽管使用五折交叉验证和中位数插补增强了证据的可信度。由于这些限制,结果的可信度中等。

analysis_zh.research_question_and_background: 本研究旨在评估支气管肺泡灌洗液(BALF)中的细胞因子和淋巴细胞谱对淋巴瘤患者下呼吸道感染(LRTIs)的诊断价值,以应对这一易感人群中对改进诊断工具的需求。
analysis_zh.study_design_and_population: 这项回顾性研究共纳入147名参与者:55名淋巴瘤合并下呼吸道感染(LRTIs)的患者,52名合并非肺部感染(NPIs)的患者,以及40名非淋巴瘤合并下呼吸道感染的患者。排除标准包括恶性实体肿瘤、其他血液系统疾病或自身免疫性疾病的诊断,以及需要长期使用特定药物的疾病。
analysis_zh.methods: 通过多参数流式细胞术分析BALF细胞因子和淋巴细胞亚群,样本在检测前按1:3比例稀释。病原学检查包括涂片染色、培养、针对SARS-CoV-2、流感A型、流感B型、呼吸道合胞病毒、腺病毒、人类鼻病毒、巨细胞病毒、EB病毒和支原体的呼吸道病毒PCR,以及宏基因组下一代测序(mNGS)。使用LASSO特征选择和五折交叉验证开发了逻辑回归模型,缺失值通过训练折的中位数进行填补。
analysis_zh.main_results: 开发了四种逻辑回归模型,测试集AUC值范围从0.845到0.973。包含CRP和SAA的基础模型整体表现优于BALF模型。
analysis_zh.interpretation_and_novelty: 作者认为,基线模型在诊断淋巴瘤患者下呼吸道感染中的表现优于BALF模型,这表明在此背景下,传统生物标志物可能比BALF细胞因子和淋巴细胞谱型更为有效。
analysis_zh.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: 这些发现可能有助于为免疫功能低下患者的下呼吸道感染(LRTIs)开发更准确的诊断策略,从而潜在改善临床决策和治疗结局。
analysis_zh.limitations_and_evidence_strength: 该研究受到其回顾性设计和潜在数据缺失的限制,尽管使用了五折交叉验证和中位数填补方法增强了证据的可信度。由于这些限制,结果的可信度中等。

analysis.event: The CDC published a report on respiratory illnesses, including Respiratory Syncytial Virus (RSV), as part of its health topics and outbreak summaries.
analysis.scale_impact_and_risk: The report highlights RSV as a significant respiratory illness, particularly in vulnerable populations such as infants and older adults. It does not provide specific case counts or risk levels for RSV.
analysis.response_status_and_uncertainty: The CDC provides general information and guidance on respiratory illnesses, including RSV, but does not indicate any specific investigation, testing, or containment measures related to RSV in the supplied evidence.

analysis.brief_en: The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) published a report on respiratory illnesses, including Respiratory Syncytial Virus (RSV), on October 9, 2026. The report is part of the CDC's broader health topics and outbreak summaries, highlighting RSV as a significant respiratory illness. It does not provide specific case counts, death counts, or risk levels for RSV, but it emphasizes the importance of monitoring and addressing such illnesses. The CDC's content includes general information and guidance on respiratory illnesses, without indicating any targeted investigation, testing, or containment measures for RSV. The report is presented as part of the CDC's public health resources, focusing on awareness and prevention strategies.

news.source_body_en: The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) published a report on respiratory illnesses, including Respiratory Syncytial Virus (RSV), on October 9, 2026. The report is part of the CDC's broader health topics and outbreak summaries, highlighting RSV as a significant respiratory illness. It does not provide specific case counts, death counts, or risk levels for RSV, but it emphasizes the importance of monitoring and addressing such illnesses. The CDC's content includes general information and guidance on respiratory illnesses, without indicating any targeted investigation, testing, or containment measures for RSV. The report is presented as part of the CDC's public health resources, focusing on awareness and prevention strategies.

news.content_title: Respiratory Syncytial Virus (RSV) News, Articles and Research
news.content: Respiratory Syncytial Virus (RSV) Nirsevimab is a long-acting monoclonal antibody that provides season-long protection against RSV in infants, reducing medically attended infections and hospitalizations. Maternal vaccination and nirsevimab together offer complementary strategies to protect newborns during their highest-risk months. Overview Feature Articles Latest Respiratory Syncytial Virus (RSV) News and Research Early-infancy infection with RSV increases the risk of developing childhood asthma Belgian scientists from VIB and Ghent University (UGent), together with Danish collaborators, have uncovered compelling evidence that early-infancy infection with respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) significantly increases the risk of developing childhood asthma-especially in children with a family history of allergy or asthma. Year-round access to RSV immunization may reduce major seasonal outbreaks Providing year-round access to RSV immunization would minimize the risk of large seasonal outbreaks across the nation, including in both urban and rural areas. Preparing for the respiratory virus season: A guide for families As respiratory virus season begins, pediatric experts are preparing for an expected rise in cases of Respiratory Syncytial Virus (RSV), which can cause cold-like symptoms in most people but serious illness in infants and older adults. COVID-19, RSV, and flu vaccines remain safe and effective The systematic review provides crucial insights into the efficacy and safety of respiratory virus vaccines, supporting evidence-based immunization practices. Study reveals impact of viral combinations on infant respiratory illness severity A new study led by researchers at National Jewish Health has revealed that, while a wide range of viruses can cause lower respiratory tract illnesses (LRIs) in infants, certain viruses and viral combinations dramatically increase the risk of severe disease. A parent's guide to manage pediatric respiratory illnesses during the virus season As we head deeper into fall and toward the holiday season, your little one may start to exhibit symptoms like a runny nose, cough, or fever. HEPA purifiers do not fully reduce classroom viral exposure In a secondary analysis of a study of 200 classrooms, Mass General Brigham researchers found respiratory viral exposures were still high in those with HEPA purifiers, suggesting additional interventions are needed. RSV vaccines protect two most-at-risk groups from severe illness The review demonstrates that vaccines for respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) are both safe and effective in protecting groups who are most at risk for serious illness, including older adults and infants. Soap shortages undermine global hand hygiene efforts A lack of soap is the most often reported barrier to effective hand hygiene-key to curbing the spread of infection-in shared community spaces, such as households, schools, and public places, finds a systematic review of the available research, published in the open access journal BMJ Global Health. RSV vaccine slashes hospitalizations in older adults in real-world trial A large, real-world randomized trial in Denmark found that the RSVpreF vaccine reduced RSV-related hospitalizations in adults aged 60 and over by over 80%. The vaccine also showed protection against broader respiratory illness with a favorable safety profile. Healthy newborns also face high risk of severe RSV infection It is not only premature babies and children with underlying diseases who suffer from serious respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) infections. Can an allergy spray help prevent COVID-19? Researchers determine the efficacy and safety of azelastine nasal spray for preventing SARS-CoV-2 infection in healthy adults. How effective is the RSV vaccine for older adults? A single dose of the RSV vaccine offers 58% protection against hospitalization in older adults, but effectiveness varies in immunocompromised individuals. New guidelines improve care for respiratory infections in leukemia patients People with leukemia have a weakened immune system due to the disease itself and treatment, which leads to an increased susceptibility to infections. RSV causes severe outcomes and heart complications in older adults Respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) is a well-known cause of infections in children, but it's understudied in older individuals. Maternal RSV vaccination linked to sharp drop in infant lung infections Vaccination of pregnant women has been linked to a drop in newborns being admitted to hospital with a serious lung infection, research suggests. Light-activated drug discovery identifies broad-spectrum antivirals UC Santa Barbara researchers and collaborators from campus biotech spinoff Integrated Biosciences, as well as Harvard, MIT and genomics company Illumina Ventures are using optogenetics - the use of light to probe the functions of living tissue - to find compounds to help our bodies more effectively help themselves in times of physiological stress. How underreporting masks the real impact of RSV in older populations Research shows RSV leads to high hospitalization rates in adults, emphasizing the importance of enhanced surveillance and diagnostic measures in healthcare. New RSV guideline aims to standardize pediatric care across China Respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) is a leading cause of acute lower respiratory infections (ALRTIs) in children under five and poses a persistent threat to child health worldwide. WHO releases first-ever position paper on immunization products to protect infants against RSV Today, the World Health Organization (WHO) published its first-ever position paper on immunization products to protect infants against respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) – the leading cause of acute lower respiratory infections in children globally

analysis.brief_en: Respiratory Syncytial Virus (RSV) remains a significant global health threat, particularly affecting infants and older adults. Early RSV infection in infancy increases the risk of childhood asthma, especially in children with a family history of allergy or asthma. For older adults, RSV causes severe outcomes and heart complications, with vaccines showing effectiveness in reducing hospitalizations by over 80% in adults aged 60 and over. Maternal vaccination and nirsevimab provide complementary protection for newborns during their highest-risk months. The WHO has issued its first position paper on RSV immunization for infants, emphasizing the need for year-round access to immunization to minimize seasonal outbreaks. Despite these advances, additional interventions are needed as HEPA purifiers alone do not fully reduce classroom viral exposure.

news.source_body_en: Respiratory Syncytial Virus (RSV) remains a significant global health threat, particularly affecting infants and older adults. Early RSV infection in infancy increases the risk of childhood asthma, especially in children with a family history of allergy or asthma. For older adults, RSV causes severe outcomes and heart complications, with vaccines showing effectiveness in reducing hospitalizations by over 80% in adults aged 60 and over. Maternal vaccination and nirsevimab provide complementary protection for newborns during their highest-risk months. The WHO has issued its first position paper on RSV immunization for infants, emphasizing the need for year-round access to immunization to minimize seasonal outbreaks. Despite these advances, additional interventions are needed as HEPA purifiers alone do not fully reduce classroom viral exposure.

(NASDAQ:ENTA), a clinical stage biotechnology company dedicated to creating novel, small molecule drugs for viral infections and immunological diseases, today announced that data for zelicapavir, its oral, once-daily, N-protein inhibitor in development for the treatment of respiratory syncytial virus (RSV), will be presented at IDWeekTM 2026 being held October 21-24, 2026 virtually and at the Walter E. Washington Convention Center in Washington, DC. Details of the presentation are as follows: Poster Title: Zelicapavir Decreases Time to Complete RSV Symptom Resolution, Hospitalization and Viral Load in a Global, Randomized, Double-Blinded, Placebo (PBO)-Controlled Phase 2 Trial of High-Risk Adults Poster Session: Novel Agents Poster Number: 3 Date: Thursday October 22, 2026 Time: 12:15 PM - 1:30 PM ET Location: Poster Hall B-C Presenter: Christopher E. Harris, M.D. The poster will be available to view on the conference platform during the conference and on the Company’s website here. Further information about IDWeekTM 2026 can be found here. About Enanta Pharmaceuticals, Inc. Enanta is using its robust, chemistry-driven approach and drug discovery capabilities to become a leader in the discovery and development of small molecule drugs for viral infections and immunological diseases. In virology, Enanta’s clinical programs are focused on the development of first-in-disease and best-in-disease treatments for respiratory syncytial virus (RSV). The Company’s immunology pipeline aims to develop treatments for inflammatory diseases by targeting key drivers of the type 2 immune response, with KIT, STAT6 and MRGPRX2 inhibition. Glecaprevir, a protease inhibitor discovered by Enanta, is part of the only treatment approved for curing both acute and chronic hepatitis C virus (HCV) infection and is sold by AbbVie in numerous countries under the tradenames MAVYRET® (U.S.) and MAVIRET® (ex-U.S.) (glecaprevir/pibrentasvir). A portion of Enanta’s royalties from HCV products developed under its collaboration with AbbVie contribute ongoing funding to Enanta’s operations. Please visit www.enanta.com for more information. news.source_body_en: Enanta Pharmaceuticals is set to present data on zelicapavir, an oral, once-daily N-protein inhibitor, at IDWeekTM 2026. The data is from a global, randomized, double-blinded, placebo-controlled Phase 2 trial targeting high-risk adults with respiratory syncytial virus (RSV). The presentation is scheduled for Thursday, October 22, 2026, at 12:15 PM to 1:30 PM ET in Poster Hall B-C at the Walter E. Washington Convention Center in Washington, DC. The conference runs from October 21-24, 2026, with virtual participation. The poster will also be available on the conference platform and the company’s website. No specific case counts, death counts, or exposure numbers are reported in the evidence, and the risk level is not explicitly stated. The event is a non-urgent update on drug development, not an outbreak or public health emergency.

(NASDAQ:ENTA), a clinical stage biotechnology company dedicated to creating novel, small molecule drugs for viral infections and immunological diseases, today announced that data for zelicapavir, its oral, once-daily, N-protein inhibitor in development for the treatment of respiratory syncytial virus (RSV), will be presented at IDWeekTM 2026 being held October 21-24, 2026 virtually and at the Walter E. Washington Convention Center in Washington, DC. Details of the presentation are as follows: Poster Title: Zelicapavir Decreases Time to Complete RSV Symptom Resolution, Hospitalization and Viral Load in a Global, Randomized, Double-Blinded, Placebo (PBO)-Controlled Phase 2 Trial of High-Risk Adults Poster Session: Novel Agents Poster Number: 3 Date: Thursday October 22, 2026 Time: 12:15 PM - 1:30 PM ET Location: Poster Hall B-C Presenter: Christopher E. Harris, M.D. The poster will be available to view on the conference platform during the conference and on the Company’s website here. Further information about IDWeekTM 2026 can be found here. About Enanta Pharmaceuticals, Inc. Enanta is using its robust, chemistry-driven approach and drug discovery capabilities to become a leader in the discovery and development of small molecule drugs for viral infections and immunological diseases. In virology, Enanta’s clinical programs are focused on the development of first-in-disease and best-in-disease treatments for respiratory syncytial virus (RSV). The Company’s immunology pipeline aims to develop treatments for inflammatory diseases by targeting key drivers of the type 2 immune response, with KIT, STAT6 and MRGPRX2 inhibition. Glecaprevir, a protease inhibitor discovered by Enanta, is part of the only treatment approved for curing both acute and chronic hepatitis C virus (HCV) infection and is sold by AbbVie in numerous countries under the tradenames MAVYRET® (U.S.) and MAVIRET® (ex-U.S.) (glecaprevir/pibrentasvir). A portion of Enanta’s royalties from HCV products developed under its collaboration with AbbVie contribute ongoing funding to Enanta’s operations. Please visit www.enanta.com for more information. If driving, slow down, use your headlights, and leave plenty of distance ahead of you. && RSV shot is a game changer, pediatricians say Alex Viveros Jackson Hole News&Guide Via Wyoming News Exchange Oct 8, 2026 Oct 8, 2026 0 Facebook Twitter WhatsApp SMS Email Vaccines are seen during the annual Cheyenne-Laramie County Public Health’s community vaccine clinic at Blue World Headquarters on Oct. 1, 2025, in Cheyenne. Wyoming Tribune Eagle/file Facebook Twitter WhatsApp SMS Email Print Copy article link Save Facebook Twitter WhatsApp SMS Email Print Copy article link Save JACKSON — Dr. Travis Riddell spent most of his pediatric career treating babies hospitalized with respiratory syncytial virus. Though the virus is extremely common, it can hit young babies hard, giving them bronchitis and outsized mucus. There’s no antiviral treatment for RSV, meaning doctors have to resort to purely supportive care. Parents around Jackson Hole may recall their infants getting sick with RSV as infants. Riddell certainly can. “My daughter, who’s now 10 years old, was in the ICU at St. John’s when she was 6 weeks old with RSV,” Riddell said. “So I’ve been there personally, on both sides of the bed.” But pediatricians have noticed a dramatic change over the last three years. In 2023, two protective RSV products — a vaccine for pregnant women and virus-fighting antibodies for infants — launched in the United States. That’s led to an outsized national decrease in RSV hospitalizations. “It really has been a game changer,” Dr. Jacqui Hardenbrook, a pediatrician at Paintbrush Pediatrics, said. “I think last winter, I only admitted two kids to the ICU.” Dr. Tiffany Milner, a pediatrician at St. John’s Health, recalls treating hospitals full of children with RSV when she started residency in Salt Lake City in 2009. That’s now changed dramatically. Across the country, RSV hospitalization dropped by as much as 71% in newborns after the shot became available, according to a 2025 study by the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. “It’s incredible,” Milner said. “It’s just so stressful as a new parent to care for a baby who is constantly coughing, and snot coming out of their nose, and having trouble feeding.” Mothers can protect their babies from RSV in two ways. They can receive a vaccine, which confers protection during their baby’s first six months of life. Babies younger than 8 months old also can receive nirsevimab or clesrovimab, which are antibodies. Antibodies are different from vaccines. Whereas vaccines contain parts of a virus — which train your body’s immune system to make antibodies that neutralize the virus — the antibody treatments fight back the virus directly. That distinction appears to have mattered for some parents, Milner said. Across the region, some parents have been hesitant to get their children vaccinated for certain diseases, amid a national anti-vaccine movement. But Milner has had patients who agree to RSV antibodies for their babies, but deny routine childhood vaccines. “People like the idea that it’s not triggering an immune response,” Milner said, “for whatever reason.” Hardenbrook also has noticed that families who refuse many childhood vaccines will sometimes elect to give their children the RSV immunization. Whereas parents may be less familiar with the devastation caused by measles and polio before vaccination, RSV’s symptoms may be more top of mind. “Almost anybody who has young kids knows somebody who’s had a kid that had RSV that was really sick,” Hardenbrook said. “People know more about it, and know how bad it can be.” Let the news come to you Get any of our free email newsletters — news headlines, sports, arts & entertainment, state legislature, CFD news, and more. (Staff File) By Adejare Atanda and Mfon Elegbede PUBLISHED: October 13, 2026 at 12:12 PM EDT Getting your Trinity Audio player ready... It’s officially fall — the mornings are sharp with cold, and the nights heavy with dew. These are perfect conditions for respiratory viruses to spread as we start to spend more time indoors. During the 2024-25 respiratory virus season, Maryland hospitals admitted 15,000 people with flu, COVID-19 or RSV (respiratory syncytial virus), and more than 1,200 of them unfortunately died. These viruses will return this fall, and we have strong tools to protect ourselves, but people are not getting clear guidance on how to apply these tools. We have updated flu and COVID-19 vaccines, RSV protections for infants and older adults that did not exist five years ago and antiviral medications to help people at high risk. However, health agencies that used to speak with one voice on vaccines are now sending mixed messages or staying silent. This has created a significant amount of uncertainty. According to a recent national survey, many people remain unclear whether specific respiratory vaccines are recommended for them. In April, Gov. Wes Moore signed the Vax Act, which directed the state health secretary to issue Maryland’s own immunization recommendations. These are grounded in the recommendations of the American Academy of Pediatrics, American Academy of Family Physicians and American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists. It is still too early to know whether this respiratory season will be mild or severe, but now is a great time to get clear on how to protect yourself and your family. Who needs what Flu, COVID-19 and RSV spread in similar ways and can cause many of the same symptoms, but they do not affect everyone equally. For example, flu can affect people of all ages, but children are especially vulnerable. COVID-19 is no longer the emergency it once was, but older adults and people who are immunocompromised still face a higher risk of severe illness. RSV is one that many adults rarely think about, yet it disproportionately affects the youngest and oldest among us. Here is how to think about the risks. If you have a baby at home, think RSV first. For your young kids, consider the flu. If you are 75 and older or immunocompromised, think COVID-19 first, then flu and RSV. And finally, if you are an adult of any age with a chronic disease, all three apply to you. For most households, the guidance for the 2026-27 respiratory virus season is simple enough to fit on an index card: 1. Everyone (6+ months). Annual flu shot, ideally by late October. 2. Adults (19-64). An updated COVID-19 vaccine this fall. 3. Adults (65+). Annual flu shot, plus the two-shot updated COVID-19 vaccine. 4. Adults (50+) with a chronic condition. A one-time RSV vaccine. 5. Pregnant individuals. Annual flu shot, the updated COVID-19 vaccine and an RSV vaccine in the third trimester. 6. Infants. Long-acting RSV antibody shot for infants less than 8 months old who are entering their first respiratory season (if the mother didn’t receive the RSV vaccine during pregnancy) 7. Immunocompromised (any age). Follow the age-appropriate guidelines above, plus an expanded COVID-19 vaccine schedule. Flu, COVID-19 and RSV vaccines can all be safely given together at one visit. They may also be given separately, but there is a downside to waiting: Every deferred shot is a shot that may never happen. Vaccines are not the whole prevention strategy Vaccines are the most effective single tool we have to stay protected against these respiratory illnesses, but they are not the entire toolbox. Part of a good plan is knowing what to do when illness arrives. Before you are sick. This is a time-tested preventive measure that is simple but effective: Wash your hands regularly. If you live in a crowded home, good air circulation is key, especially with at-risk groups — newborns, frail older adults, pregnant women and those with immune disorders. Open your windows, run the HVAC fan and consider a portable HEPA filter. In addition, stock up on at-home viral test kits and fitted masks. Finally, keep a list of important phone numbers and addresses handy, including your doctor’s office, urgent care centers and the nearest emergency department. When you get sick. As soon as symptoms start, make those calls and get tested promptly — early treatment is key, depending on the infection — and stay away from at-risk people or mask if you must be around others. Although the U.S. Constitution’s Supremacy Clause gives valid federal law priority over conflicting state law, states continue to have broad authority over public health matters, and Maryland has taken advantage of this through the Vax Act to address gaps in federal vaccine guidance. Let’s be clear about what this law does and does not do. It does not create any mandates: Flu, COVID-19 and RSV vaccines are not required for school, childcare or work, and existing school-entry rules and exemptions remain unchanged. Rather, the law ties two practical allowances to Maryland’s recommendations rather than to federal guidance. Pharmacists can give flu and COVID-19 vaccines without a prescription to anyone 3 years and older. And coverage by state-regulated health plans is tied to the state’s recommendations, so that if federal recommendations narrow, Maryland’s coverage does not have to follow. The insurance protection concern is real. HHS’s latest move could disenfranchise children from lower-income households. Because of federal rules, children covered by Medicaid won’t be able to access vaccines that are no longer recommended by the federal government, even as children with private insurance will. So what should Marylanders actually do? Here are five things: 1. Check vaccine recommendations for your household on the state’s childhood and adult schedules. Your source is health.maryland.gov/recommendedvaccines. When there is conflicting advice or guidance, defer to Maryland’s. 2. If you can, book a single visit. And make that this month. Flu, COVID-19 and RSV shots can be given together. 3. If you are pregnant or expecting a baby this winter, discuss RSV with your doctor now. The window to receive the maternal RSV vaccine is narrow. If needed, check with your pediatrician’s office about availability of the RSV antibody for your infant. 4. If you are older, especially with a chronic condition, request the RSV vaccine. Age and chronic conditions are qualifying in Maryland. 5. Make a sick-day plan in advance. This should include telephone numbers and physical addresses of clinicians and telehealth services for when you get sick. With flu activity rising earlier than usual in parts of the country and COVID-19 still elevated, this is a good time to move vaccinations off your “I’ll get around to it” list. Marylanders already do better than most of the country. In 2024-25, 63% of Maryland children and 74% of Marylanders older adults were vaccinated against flu, roughly 10 points above the national figures. This is encouraging. However, during the same season, more than a third of the state’s children went unprotected, and many older Marylanders eligible for the RSV vaccine never received it. With the possibility of a future “twindemic” or “tripledemic” caused by high cases of flu, COVID-19 or RSV that could overwhelm healthcare systems and resources, it is critical for all of us to do our part. The viruses are ones we know, and the tools are better than they have ever been. Maryland has drawn the roadmap, but the rest is up to us. Protect yourself, protect your family and go get those shots. Dr. Adejare Atanda is a health policy researcher and former infectious disease epidemiologist at the Maryland Department of Health. Dr. Mfon Elegbede is a pediatrician and public health expert. Both are Maryland residents. Blue Lake Biotechnology To Present Data For RSV Vaccine Candidate BLB201 In A Late-Breaking Presentation At ISV Annual Congress PR Newswire Mon, October 12, 2026 at 5:59 AM PDT 2 min read ATHENS, Ga. and SAN JOSE, Calif., Oct. 12, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Blue Lake Biotechnology, Inc., a clinical-stage intranasal vaccine company developing parainfluenza virus 5 (PIV5)-vectored vaccines that harness the full breadth of the immune system to protect against serious infectious diseases, today announced that interim data from the company's Phase 1/2a pediatric clinical trial of RSV vaccine candidate BLB201 will be presented as a late-breaking abstract during the International Society for Vaccines 2026 Annual Congress in Antwerp, Belgium. The oral presentation will include updated safety and immunogenicity data from both RSV-seronegative and RSV-seropositive children ranging in age from eight to 59 months. Presentation Details Title: PIV5-vectored Intranasal RSV Vaccine is Safe and Immunogenic in Infants and Young Children Date/Time: October 12, 2026 17:20 CET Presenter: Biao He, Ph.D., CEO, Blue Lake Biotechnology About RSV and BLB201 Respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) is a highly contagious virus that infects over 64 million people worldwide each year. While RSV typically causes mild, cold-like symptoms, it can cause severe and potentially life-threatening disease in infants, older adults, the immunocompromised, and people with certain chronic health conditions. In the U.S., RSV causes up to 80,000 hospitalizations among children under five and up to 160,000 among older adults annually, with up to 10,000 deaths. BLB201 is an intranasal RSV vaccine candidate being evaluated in Phase 1/2a clinical testing in children ages eight to 59 months. Interim data have indicated that BLB201 may prevent symptomatic RSV infection in young children. BLB201 has received Fast Track designation from the U.S. Food and Drug Administration for prevention of RSV-associated acute respiratory disease in adults over 60 and pediatric populations. BLB201 uses a proprietary PIV5 vector to express the RSV-F protein. PIV5 has been used for decades in canine vaccines and is not known to cause human disease. About Blue Lake Biotechnology Blue Lake Biotechnology, Inc. and affiliate CyanVac LLC are developing intranasal vaccines designed to activate mucosal, systemic, and cellular immunity. Our proprietary PIV5 platform mimics natural infection while expressing proteins from targeted pathogens. Our clinical-stage pipeline includes vaccines designed to prevent respiratory infections and overcome limitations of existing vaccine technologies. Learn more at Blue Lake Biotechnology. risk Summary Key Takeaways: The RSV virus can cause severe respiratory illness, hospitalization, and even death, especially in infants and older adults. RSV vaccination is recommended for adults 75 and older, and some adults ages 50–74 with higher-risk health conditions. Pregnant women or newborns can receive preventive protection during RSV season, helping reduce the risk of severe illness. Respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) often looks like a common cold, but it’s a virus that can have much more serious consequences, especially for babies and older adults. A vaccine offers protection for people at greatest risk. And for older people, it can be a one-time shot rather than an annual vaccination. Talha Khan, MD, a family medicine physician at OSF HealthCare, says RSV is a common respiratory virus that can affect people of all ages. Young infants and older adults are among those most likely to develop severe illness. “It can cause pretty severe respiratory infection that can lead to hospitalization and even death, so it is something we don’t take lightly. And we do have a vaccine for it now. So we do recommend getting that vaccine, if they’re eligible, so they have that extra layer of protection.” For adults, the RSV vaccine is recommended for everyone age 75 and older. “It can be given to individuals who are younger than that – age 50 to 74 – if they have some chronic conditions: respiratory disease, things like COPD, asthma, heart disease and if they’re a current smoker. All those things put them at increased risk for a more severe infection.” For infants, RSV can be particularly dangerous during the virus’s typical fall and winter season. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention points out it is the number one cause of hospitalization among infants in the U.S. The RSV vaccine can offer preventive protection when given to the baby after birth. “And then it’s also recommended for pregnant women if they’re pregnant during that respiratory virus season [September-January], as well. They recommend either pregnant women get it or the infant gets it once their born, typically not both.” During a particularly bad respiratory virus season in 2022, OSF OnCall launched a free, at-home monitoring service for babies and toddlers up to five years old. The digital service continues today and includes an at-home care kit and easy access to a real-time chat. If necessary, a video visit is an option for parents or guardians of an infant or young child with any respiratory illness, including RSV. While RSV is common, many older adults may not be as familiar with the vaccine as they are with annual flu or COVID-19 shots. “A few of my patients have kind of brought up that, ‘Oh, that’s one of the vaccines I’ve never heard of,’” says Dr. Khan. “But, again, it is important because it can cause those severe respiratory infections, [including] pneumonia, and potentially even lead to death. So, if we can stop that or stop you from getting a serious infection with a one-time vaccine, then why not just get that done.” For people who may qualify for the vaccine, health providers recommend talking with a health care professional about their individual risk factors and the best way to protect against severe RSV. With a single dose offering long-term protection, the decision may be one that is easier to make than most people realize. Dr. Talha Khan is a family medicine physician at OSF HealthCare in Bloomington, Illinois. Topics & Projects Antimicrobial Stewardship Chronic Wasting Disease Osterholm Update Podcasts Newsletters About CIDRAP CIDRAP in the News Our Staff Our Director Osterholm in the Press Shop Merchandise Contact Us About Search CLOSE Search Support Menu Maternal RSV vaccine is effective, but few women opt for it, new data reveal Meghan Holohan Respiratory Syncytial Virus (RSV) Wirestock / iStock Share Copied to clipboard While respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) remains so common that almost every child gets it before they turn 2 years old, it can cause serious illness in infants, leading to the hospitalization of up to three of every 100 infected infants. Maternal vaccination with RSVpreF (Abrysvo) protects newborns from getting the virus, yet relatively few moms in the United States and Europe have opted for it since its rollout in 2023, a study published last week in The Lancet Regional Health-Europe finds. “We found the vaccine reduced the risk of RSV-related hospitalization in babies under six months by around 74%, which lines up well with what the clinical trials predicted,” senior author Ting Shi, PhD, MPH, of the University of Edinburgh’s Usher Institute, said in a university news release. “But uptake during the first vaccination seasons was low.” 19% to 50% vaccine uptake Researchers from the University of Edinburgh and the University of Granada in Spain led the study, which examined data from 16 studies from the United States, the United Kingdom, and France. The studies included more than 4 million pregnancies in 2023-24 and 2024-25. Thirteen studies took place in the United States, where 27.1% of pregnant women accepted the maternal RSV vaccine. One cross-sectional study in England showed a 19% maternal RSV vaccine uptake, while a study in Scotland indicated 50.4% of women received the dose. The French study showed that the rate of acceptance among moms-to-be was about the same as it was in the United States: 27.2%. Women who received other vaccines recommended during pregnancy were more likely to accept the RSVpreF vaccine, which works best if administered from 32 to 36 weeks’ gestation. We found the vaccine reduced the risk of RSV-related hospitalization in babies under six months by around 74%, which lines up well with what the clinical trials predicted. Ting Shi, PhD, MPH The scientists also looked at data about how well the RSV vaccine worked and discovered that it was 73.6% effective against hospitalization for babies 6 months or younger. “Research shows that RSV vaccination during pregnancy protects babies,” Evelyn Balsells, PhD, MPH, of the University of Granada, said in the news release. “Efforts to increase uptake and reduce disparities will be essential to maximize the benefits of maternal RSV vaccination.” Need for proactive rather than reactive strategy An accompanying editorial addressed low vaccine coverage in the European Union and the need to bolster maternal vaccination rates across the continent. “Maternal vaccination protects infants during the most clinically vulnerable first months, before they are eligible for routine childhood vaccinations, but uptake of many maternal vaccines remains low despite strong evidence of efficacy and safety,” the authors wrote. The authors suggested several strategies, including better coordination among medical specialties when it comes to recommending and providing vaccines, outreach to areas where structural barriers lead to low vaccination rates, better surveillance of diseases and vaccine coverage, and a proactive instead of reactive vaccine strategy. “Europe should not wait for the next maternal vaccine to be licensed before addressing these systemic weaknesses,” they added.
